docs.title: Event Timing Engineering Portal
docs.text:
This is the event-timing engineering portal. It is a derived reader over the same engineering source that produces the existing Book and traceability evidence.

  • Source revision: 62abf8caa7a280cc46d701e8c3802c7255cb011f
  • Engineering objects: 272
  • Authored relations: 421

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Engineering explorer — keep the real SI-01 architecture visible while inspecting one selected engineering object.
  • Traceability comparison — keep one engineering object fixed on the left while opening related objects on the right.
  • Engineering object index — searchable generated object pages with readable, direction-aware relationship headings.
  • Engineering Client UI — review the Step-4 Timing UI wireframes and state/interaction design.
  • Architecture Book — the existing assembled Book remains a first-class output and is not owned by this portal.

The portal does not author engineering meaning. Stable IDs, relations and content come from native MyST/Sphinx-Needs and the released normalized graph boundary.

docs.text:
The existing assembled architecture Book remains the linear reading/review output.

Open the generated Architecture Book

The Material portal complements that Book with search, object pages and focused engineering context. It does not replace Book assembly or source ownership.

docs.title: Engineering Client — Step 4 Timing UI
docs.text:
This is a derived portal view of the D01 mid-fidelity UI baseline. The authoritative design text and control/state rules remain in SDE03 — Engineering Client.

The wireframes are generated from declarative YAML by tool.eng-docs; the same sources also produce editable draw.io output in the normal documentation publication.

docs.title: CLOSED without operational location
docs.text: Set Location is available; Open waits for an authoritative assigned LocationId.

docs.title: OPEN with bounded LogBook
docs.text: Location is fixed; dev auto-reg is capability-gated and committed records are shown from the LogBook.

docs.title: RECONNECTING / stale
docs.text: Cached state remains visible while controls stay disabled until rebuild and dedup complete.

docs.text:
The Engineering Explorer keeps the generated SI-01 architecture on the left and the selected engineering object on the right. Selecting an architecture element or an object below updates the right-hand detail pane without replacing the architecture context.

For relation-by-relation comparison, use the separate Traceability comparison workspace.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Java design for AntennaManager, Antenna implementations, optional PowerDevice control, inventory lifecycle and SimulatedAntenna behaviour.

The Java antenna boundary separates device lifecycle from decoded observation processing.

docs.title: Antenna and manager
docs.text:
Antenna represents one configured logical antenna/device capability. It owns the decoded observation event and provider-specific device/session mechanics needed for startup self-test, initialization and inventory control.

The application-facing and device-facing lifecycle words are kept distinct. TimingNode uses OPEN / CLOSED; antenna/provider cleanup uses shutdown() rather than close() so device cleanup is not confused with TimingNode state.

Illustrative provider shape:

interface Antenna {
    AntennaInfo selfTest();

    void initialize();

    void startInventory();

    void stopInventory();

    boolean inventoryRunning();

    void shutdown();

    EventSource<TagObservation> tagObservedEvent();
}

selfTest() is the startup device check and has PASS/FAIL semantics at manager level. It may return decoded identity/version information for diagnostics, but SI-01 does not model a parallel antenna status model merely to represent startup progress. initialize() prepares the provider for normal use. startInventory() and stopInventory() control observation delivery. shutdown() releases provider resources and remains valid when initialization did not complete successfully.

docs.title: Coordination ownership
docs.text:
TimingSystem behaviour and I/O device mechanics are separate:

application.ApplicationConductor
      |
      +--> AntennaManager lifecycle
      |
      +--> domain.system.TimingSystemConductor lifecycle
              |
              +--> TimingNode lifecycle (1..N)
              |
              +--> node states -> shared inventory demand
                            |
                            v
                      AntennaManager
                      inventory / device mechanics
      |
      +--> AntennaSet
      |       +--> ManagedAntenna(s)
      |               +--> Antenna
      |               +--> optional PowerDevice
      |
      +--> reusable SelfTestTask
      +--> reusable InventoryTask
      +--> reusable AntennaShutdownTask

domain.system.TimingSystemConductor calls AntennaManager.setInventoryRequired(anyNodeOpen) on its system's optional manager. It does not issue device-mechanism commands such as power-on, initialize, power-cycle or antenna switching. domain.system.TimingSystem owns the lifecycle ordering between the AntennaManager and the system Conductor.

AntennaManager is the single controller for the configured 1..N antenna capability of one TimingSystem. It owns lifecycle/status, the requested/applied inventory setting and one explicit manager control state machine. It owns the three reusable task objects directly. The physical multi-step sequences live in those task classes under manager/task. The task classes work directly on manager-owned ManagedAntenna objects; there is no second task-facing antenna interface.

AntennaManager may keep one private Setting<Boolean> for inventory reconciliation:

requestedValue
appliedValue
changePending = requestedValue != appliedValue
requestRevision = identity of the latest explicit request

Setting is passive bookkeeping and owns no executor, lifecycle, retry policy or device action. A single inventory demand does not justify a shared setting key, grouped transaction or setting-change event. AntennaManager calls markApplied(value) only after the corresponding task has completed successfully. A newer request may therefore arrive while an older transition is executing; once the older transition completes, changePending still exposes whether another transition is needed.

Device objects and configuration remain separate concepts. Antenna and PowerDevice are device objects. AntennaSet is the composition-time collection that binds those device objects to stable AntennaId values and stores the optional external power stabilization value. Multiplex membership and switch interval are configured once at set level. There is deliberately no per-antenna AntennaInstallation value.

Activating AntennaManager starts one reusable SelfTestTask for the complete antenna set. The manager does not contain the per-antenna self-test sequence and does not wait for provider I/O. The task performs one physical action per turn, releases the shared worker during real stabilization waits and publishes one completion event when the complete round finishes. Presentation startup can therefore continue while self-test is in progress.

docs.title: Temporary Windows development default
docs.text:
Until the normal runtime mapper composes the full IF-11 antenna configuration, the Windows development platform uses one explicit fallback so AntennaManager is exercised by the normal executable:

PlatformEnvironment = WINDOWS
and no explicit antenna composition available yet
        |
        v
1 -> built-in SimulatedAntenna
        + optional SimulatedPowerDevice
        |
        v
normal AntennaManager
        |
        v
asynchronous self-test + inventory intent

This fallback is a development/platform default, not a silent physical-reader substitute. Startup logging must state clearly that the Windows default selected a simulated antenna and that no physical RFID reader is in use. On non-Windows platforms, no antenna configuration continues to mean no AntennaManager.

Operating-system identity is exposed once through PlatformEnvironment; Runtime and Application code must not scatter direct System.getProperty("os.name") checks.

Explicit IF-11 antenna configuration takes precedence as soon as that mapper/composition path is implemented. The fallback does not redefine the IF-11 antenna schema or provider selection rules.

docs.title: Startup self-test
docs.text:
Startup self-test is one manager-owned cooperative task:

ComponentLifecycleManager
        |
        v
AntennaManager.onActivate()
        |
        v
SelfTestTask

for each ManagedAntenna:
    POWER_ON
       |
       +-- AFTER(stabilization)
       v
    provider selfTest
       |
       +-- AGAIN
       v
    POWER_OFF
       |
       v
next antenna

round complete
       |
       v
selfTestCompletedEvent(result)
       |
       v
AntennaManager

self-test round complete -> manager ready for later control
individual PASS/FAIL results remain diagnostic

The configured stabilization interval is an actual physical wait and therefore uses AFTER(delay). The task owns the round and its execution handle. AntennaManager subscribes once to the task completion event; it does not keep the task Future or duplicate the per-antenna progress state. The current provider call may still be synchronous within one task turn. A future provider may use callbacks, bounded polling or its own internal execution without changing the manager contract.

Startup self-test result and normal operating state remain separate. The antenna operation state is limited to the lifecycle needed for normal control:

INACTIVE -> PREPARING -> READY -> INVENTORY
                              |
                              +--> stop -> READY

shutdown -> INACTIVE

After a successful self-test with external power removed, the antenna is therefore self-test PASS + INACTIVE, not artificially READY.

docs.title: TimingNode-driven inventory actions
docs.text:
SI01-REQ-053 uses one system-scoped inventory demand:

TimingNode A/B/... PROPERTIES.CHANGED
       |
       v
wake domain.system.TimingSystemConductor control task
       |
       v
read node.functionalState() for all nodes
       |
       v
inventoryRequired = any node OPEN
       |
       v
AntennaManager.setInventoryRequired(inventoryRequired)
       |
       v
AntennaManager wakes and reconciles desired versus applied state
       |
       v
InventoryTask -> managed antennas / optional power

An unchanged desired value does not schedule a new attempt. Explicit repeated requestEnableInventory() / requestDisableInventory() calls are separate retry attempts. AntennaManager owns all physical mechanics: self-test, power, initialization, multiplexing and shutdown. Runtime separately wires antenna observations to configured TimingNode TagProcessors. Per-antenna commands and individual cycling are future roadmap features; internal multiplex rotation already works.

docs.title: Failure and recovery ownership
docs.text:
While inventory remains required, a runtime device failure does not change the application intent. AntennaManager owns any recovery/reinitialization process needed to restore the requested state:

inventory enable remains requested
        |
        v
runtime antenna/provider failure
        |
        v
AntennaManager records failure
        |
        +--> stop/clean up failed operation
        +--> optional power cycle
        +--> stabilization / self-test or readiness check as required
        +--> reinitialize
        +--> resume inventory when usable

Conductor does not micromanage that recovery sequence and does not need to resend the same OPEN-derived intent after every provider failure. The exact automatic retry trigger, retry limit, delay/backoff and terminal-failure policy remain an open detailed-design decision and must be tied to an explicit requirement before implementation adds that policy.

docs.title: Execution and delayed device work
docs.text:
AntennaManager owns one SerialTaskRunner backed by Runtime's sharedIoScheduledExecutor. The runner executes the manager's reusable main task and child tasks. Delayed task steps use the JDK scheduler as a timer and submit the same task run's next eligible step directly to that scheduler. Waiting consumes no runner pending-step slot. This adds no per-manager physical thread or second logical queue.

Runtime-owned sharedIoScheduledExecutor
                 |
                 v
         SerialTaskRunner
          AntennaManager
                 |
          +------+------+------+
          |             |      |
          v             v      v
   SelfTestTask   InventoryTask AntennaShutdownTask
          \             |      /
           \            v     /
              ManagedAntenna(s)
                 |
                 +--> Antenna
                 +--> optional PowerDevice

Each cooperative task executes one logical step per turn and returns AGAIN, AFTER(delay), AWAIT(completion) or DONE. AGAIN yields by submitting the next step at the back of the executor queue. AFTER(delay) uses a timer registration and does not occupy the physical worker while waiting. AWAIT releases the worker until an asynchronous dependency completes.

For antenna control, one task turn corresponds to at most one direct physical device action. AntennaManager owns one reusable self-test task, one reusable inventory task and one reusable shutdown task directly.

Representative state machines are:

SelfTestTask
  POWER_ON -> AFTER(stabilization) -> SELF_TEST -> POWER_OFF -> next antenna -> event

InventoryTask
  requested OFF:
    STOP_INVENTORY -> POWER_OFF -> applied=false

  requested ON:
    POWER_ON -> AFTER(stabilization) -> INITIALIZE -> START_INVENTORY
    -> applied=true

  multiplex while requested ON:
    WAIT(interval) -> STOP_CURRENT -> START_NEXT -> WAIT(interval)

The inventory task re-reads the requested Setting<Boolean> on each turn. A changed request therefore changes the next direction of the same long-lived state machine rather than causing a second inventory controller or a new enable/disable task object to be constructed.

A synchronous provider method such as selfTest(), initialize(), startInventory() or stopInventory() still occupies the worker for the duration of that call. Cooperative scheduling cannot make a blocking provider API non-blocking. A real provider must therefore either use bounded device/protocol I/O for such a step or expose staged readiness/completion mechanics that its own cooperative state machine can use.

The generic manager runner does not justify a second timeout thread merely to interrupt an unknown future provider implementation. Exact provider-operation timeout/cancellation semantics are deferred until a real antenna provider establishes what its serial/network API can guarantee. Whatever mechanism is chosen must not block the shared worker waiting for work that still needs that same worker or serial lane to execute.

A concrete antenna/provider implementation may itself use cooperative tasks when one device operation consists of multiple protocol commands, waits, retries or readiness checks. If isolation requires a device-specific logical lane, that lane may still use the same Runtime-owned physical I/O worker. This preserves ordering/isolation without creating one operating-system thread per antenna.

Concrete Antenna construction is passive. Creating and wiring a provider object must not start inventory or hidden background activity.

docs.title: External power
docs.text:
External power switching is optional and modelled as a separate PowerDevice. Composition may bind an antenna to a power device plus a stabilization duration. The manager task can then order power-on before self-test/initialize, yield for stabilization, and power-off when the antenna is no longer required.

PowerDevice remains separate from Antenna. A physical reader may be powered through a relay board, GPIO-controlled supply or another installation component unrelated to the reader vendor protocol. A provider that owns its power mechanism internally may omit the external device.

docs.title: Multiplex switching
docs.text:
One AntennaManager supports zero or one inventory mutual-exclusion group. Antennas outside that group operate independently. The group contains 2..N configured antennas that may not inventory simultaneously.

SI01-REQ-054 requires only this behaviour:

inventory group required
        |
        v
start first available member

every configured interval:
        current member inventory OFF
                    |
                    v
        next healthy member inventory ON
                    |
                    +--> failed/unavailable member: skip

At most one healthy group member inventories at a time. A failed member is skipped without stopping healthy members.

The switch is fail-safe when stopping the currently active member fails. Because that reader may still be inventorying, AntennaSwitchTask must not start another group member. The failed stop is recorded on the current antenna and normal recovery/diagnostics handle the fault; mutual exclusion takes priority over continuing round-robin rotation.

There is deliberately no separate switching controller. AntennaSwitchTask owns the small amount of switch-local state: phase, current/next selection and interval wait. It is one reusable state-machine object owned directly by AntennaManager and reset before a new switching run.

The task does not own startup self-test, power preparation, antenna initialization, manager-wide status, requested/applied inventory state or generic scheduling mechanics. Those remain with their existing owners.

The public/reference baseline remains the known two-antenna group with a 500 ms interval. The number of configured antennas does not by itself justify more physical I/O workers; V01 runtime characterization remains the authority for increasing physical parallelism.

The built-in SimulatedAntenna path models the same lifecycle contract. Simulation includes explicit powered/unpowered state when paired with simulated power control, initialization/inventory preconditions and controllable self-test/initialize/start failures so startup containment, recovery design and multiplex behaviour can be verified without hardware.

docs.title: TagObservation and local event delivery
docs.text:
TagObservation is an immutable decoded input fact:

final class TagObservation {
    TagId tagId();
    int rssi();
    long observedAtEpochMillis();
    long observedAtMonotonicNanos();
}

The antenna/provider implementation owns vendor bytes, framing, encryption and decryption. Once that work is complete, the generic observation carries the semantic domain.eventdata.TagId. RSSI is the decoded/normalized signal strength used by TagProcessor policy.

Both time bases are captured at the earliest accepted decoded-observation point. The absolute epoch-millisecond value becomes the registration's source event time when that observation is selected. The monotonic value is never persisted; it only decides passage gaps/duration and equal-RSSI ordering. A presentation or protocol boundary may materialize a semantic timestamp object when that representation is actually needed.

Each antenna owns:

private final Event<TagObservation> observationEvent = new Event<>();

public EventSource<TagObservation> tagObservedEvent() {
    return observationEvent;
}

Provider callbacks perform only bounded observation ingress. EventData resolution, duplicate suppression, passage filtering, diagnostics and TimingNode queueing run through TagProcessor's typed observation SerialLane and direct scheduled callbacks on the same Runtime-owned single-thread executor.

docs.title: Optional raw-observation persistence
docs.text:
Raw tag-observation logging is a separate non-critical consumer of EventSource<TagObservation>. It does not sit inline between Antenna and TagProcessor.

The Java shape is a bounded asynchronous sink:

Antenna Event<TagObservation>
       |
       +--> TagProcessor --> TimingNode.onNewRegistration(...) --> LogBook.execute(...)
       |
       +--> RawTagObservationSink
              |
              +-- bounded local buffer
              +-- non-blocking offer on callback thread
              |
              v
        shared bounded I/O ExecutorService
              |
              v
        append/rotate diagnostic observation store

Do not submit one unbounded executor task per observation. The sink owns a bounded buffer and schedules/drains work through the shared executor so a burst of raw observations cannot fill the executor queue with arbitrary numbers of tiny persistence tasks.

Required behaviour:

  • observation callback performs only a bounded/non-blocking buffer offer;
  • one sink keeps at most one drain job queued or running; new observations go only into that sink's bounded local buffer;
  • a drain job processes a bounded batch before returning to the shared I/O executor;
  • stored records preserve the immutable observation values exactly enough for diagnostics;
  • queue-full/drop count is observable;
  • storage/write failures are observable;
  • diagnostic logging failure does not change TagProcessor queueing or TimingData commit;
  • shutdown performs a bounded drain according to the configured diagnostic-retention policy and then closes the store;
  • raw observation files are explicitly non-authoritative and may be rotated/retained independently from TimingData.

A concrete sink may bind source/antenna identity from the subscription/composition context when that is needed for diagnostics; D04 does not require source identity to be added to the generic TagObservation value merely for logging.

docs.title: Tag processing
docs.text:
The node-local tag-processing path is:

TagProcessor
  -> EventData.registrationIdFor(TagId)
  -> RegistrationDuplicateFilter
  -> TagObservationFilter
       keyed by RegistrationId
       retains per-TagId passage attribution
  -> TimingNode.onNewRegistration(...)
  -> LogBook.execute(...)

TagProcessor.onTagObserved(...) is the Antenna EventSource callback. It only tries to place the immutable observation in its bounded queue and returns. Mapping, filtering and diagnostics do not run on the provider callback thread.

On the TagProcessor lane, EventData first resolves the semantic TagId to a RegistrationId. Unmapped observations are counted and discarded. Duplicate suppression is then checked by RegistrationId. Only registrations that still need processing enter passage aggregation.

One participant/registration may have multiple physical tags. The passage filter therefore remains keyed by RegistrationId:

TAG-A -> R-123 --+
                  +--> one R-123 passage
TAG-B -> R-123 --+

It does not maintain independent passage or duplicate windows per tag.

docs.title: Registration passage state
docs.text:
A high-rate reader may report many observations during one physical passage. Keep one small mutable passage state per active RegistrationId. In addition to expiry and strongest-observation state, retain compact per-tag attribution:

PassageState R-123
  firstSeenNanos
  lastSeenNanos

  TAG-A
    observationCount
    strongestRssi
    first/last observed time

  TAG-B
    observationCount
    strongestRssi
    first/last observed time

  selected
    TagId
    strongestRssi
    observedAtEpochMillis

The implementation need not retain every TagObservation. Per-tag counters/extrema are sufficient for the baseline diagnostic requirement.

A passage closes when either condition becomes true:

now - lastSeen >= quietTimeout
OR
now - firstSeen >= maxBurstDuration

The selected candidate is the strongest observation over the complete RegistrationId passage, regardless of which associated TagId produced it. Equal RSSI keeps the earlier selected observation unless later requirements define another rule.

The selected observation's original absolute epoch-millisecond value is emitted through TagProcessor.NewRegistration and remains a primitive through TimingNode and LogBookCommands. The default IF-05 profile canonicalizes that value to its required centisecond effective-time precision only when creating the TimingRecord.

docs.title: Duplicate suppression and queueing
docs.text:
The filtering order is:

TagObservation(TagId, RSSI, observedAtEpochMillis, observedAtMonotonicNanos)
  |
  +--> EventData.registrationIdFor(TagId)
          |
          +--> no RegistrationId ----------------------> unmapped
          |
          +--> RegistrationDuplicateFilter ------------> duplicate
          |
          +--> TagObservationFilter
                  keyed by RegistrationId
                  per-TagId attribution
                  strongest observation
                  |
                  +--> selected registration
                          |
                          +--> record RegistrationId duplicate window
                          +--> emit TagProcessor.NEW_REGISTRATION
                                  |
                                  +--> TimingNode OPEN -> LogBook.execute(...)
                                  +--> TimingNode CLOSED -> ignore registration

The duplicate window belongs to TagProcessor's accepted passage selection, before the fire-and-forget TimingNode/LogBook handoff. LogBook.execute(...) has no admission result: it returns after attempting to queue the command and reports a later queue rejection only as a LogBook diagnostic. A persistence/admission failure therefore does not reopen TagProcessor's duplicate window. Once R-123 is suppressed, observations from TAG-A and TAG-B are both suppressed because EventData resolves both to the same RegistrationId.

docs.title: Engineering diagnostic view
docs.text:
TagProcessor exposes an immutable read-only diagnostic snapshot of pending/recent passage processing. It is intended for engineering presentation and may contain:

  • RegistrationId;
  • contributing TagIds;
  • observation count per TagId;
  • strongest RSSI per TagId;
  • selected TagId, RSSI and observed time;
  • first/last observation timing;
  • processing state/outcome where retained.

The snapshot is not TimingData, is not authoritative commit state and does not allow mutation of TagProcessor. It may be sampled/published through the normal Presentation path without making the engineering client part of timing processing.

docs.title: Execution and housekeeping
docs.text:
TagProcessor owns one bounded SerialLane<TagObservation>. Its observationQueueCapacity is the capacity of that lane; there is no separate observation buffer in front of another lane.

Runtime supplies one single-thread tagProcessorScheduledExecutor. That same executor backs the observation lane and is also the processor's direct JDK ScheduledExecutorService for timed work. Passage-filter sweeps and duplicate-state housekeeping use scheduleWithFixedDelay(...) only while timed state exists. Policy changes use scheduler.execute(...). Because all of those callbacks and the observation lane worker use the same physical thread, mutable TagProcessor state remains serialized without a scheduled-lane wrapper or tick-item queue.

No timer/scheduled task is created per observation and no dedicated thread is created per TagProcessor.

The processor constructor receives EventData and the Runtime-owned scheduler rather than a loose mapper or scheduled-lane wrapper:

TagProcessor(
    EventData eventData,
    ReadOnlyConfiguration<TagProcessingPolicy> policyConfiguration,
    MonotonicClock monotonicClock,
    TagProcessingMetrics metrics,
    ScheduledExecutorService scheduler)

TimingApplicationRuntime.create(...) does not expose a separate tag-to-registration mapper parameter. Normal and simulated compositions construct/use EventData and then use the same TagProcessor path.

TagProcessingPolicy continues to own quiet timeout, maximum passage duration, registration duplicate window, sweep cadence and bounded observation-lane capacity. Runtime policy replacement remains serialized by submitting it to the same single-thread scheduler.

docs.title: SimulatedAntenna
docs.text:
SimulatedAntenna implements the same lifecycle and observation contract. It can be probed/initialized, inventory can be enabled/disabled and deterministic TagObservation values can be emitted only while inventory is active.

It owns no TimingNode, mapper, filter or persistence shortcut. Its only test/simulation specific capability is deterministic control of the decoded observations it publishes.

docs.title: Simulated tag scenarios
docs.text:
The simulated antenna remains deliberately passive. Behaviour such as repeated reads, one-versus-two-tag passages, RSSI shape and passage duration belongs to a separate engineering simulation layer rather than to SimulatedAntenna itself.

The Application-facing engineering boundary is:

SimulationControl
  startRegistration(registrationId, profileId)

SimulationControl is optional and capability-gated. Runtime supplies it only when the composition has a controllable SimulatedAntenna. The API adapter calls this narrow boundary; it never receives the SimulatedAntenna object and never calls TagProcessor or TimingNode directly.

The Runtime implementation, named SimulatedTagScenarioRunner, owns:

  • the selected SimulatedAntenna;
  • the same immutable EventData used by TagProcessor;
  • a shared TimeSource for observation timestamps;
  • one bounded scheduled execution capability supplied by Runtime.

For one request it resolves EventData.tagIdsFor(registrationId), chooses the requested profile and emits that profile's TagObservation sequence through the simulated antenna. No second TagId-to-RegistrationId mapping is introduced. A missing registration mapping, inactive simulated antenna or unavailable profile is an explicit rejected simulation request.

Delayed observations use the shared scheduled-execution mechanism and release the physical worker between observations; profile delays must not be implemented with sleeps on the shared I/O worker. Multiple accepted scenarios may therefore interleave according to their scheduled observation times while still using bounded Runtime-owned execution.

Initial built-in profile ids are:

  • simple — one minimal deterministic passage, using the first mapped tag;
  • normal — a representative clean passage and both mapped tags when at least two are available;
  • edge — a deterministic edge-shape family including short, long and single-tag behaviour. The selected edge shape is derived deterministically from the requested RegistrationId so the same request is repeatable.

Exact RSSI values, observation counts and relative offsets are implementation/test-fixture data, not Domain or IF-05 semantics. Tests assert the intended shape and resulting TagProcessor behaviour without promoting those fixture numbers into product requirements.

For normal standalone development, the public synthetic EventData provider id simulation reuses the default/reference identifier convention for normal registrations RT-A-0001 through RT-A-2000. Each registration resolves from the matching physical pair TT-A-NNNN-1 and TT-A-NNNN-2. This keeps simulation behaviour representative without introducing a second synthetic identity grammar. Reserve scenarios may use RT-R-NNNN only when the required TeamId assignment is supplied by the scenario/reference data.

The Development Client composes batches from the single-scenario IF-03 operation. Batch state stays client-side: count, numeric range, ascending versus seedable pseudo-random selection and interval between registration starts. The interval is deliberately outside the profile: the profile owns observation timing inside one passage.

docs.title: DD-CooperativeExecution — Cooperative execution and TimingSystem coordination
docs.text:
Type: Detailed Design Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Java design for cooperative task execution and the TimingSystem-scoped coordination pattern used by domain.system.TimingSystemConductor.

Both coordinators are labeled Conductor in Figure SI01-01, one in the Application layer and one inside TimingSystem. Their Java implementations are application.ApplicationConductor and domain.system.TimingSystemConductor.

Some operations consist of several ordered steps. One step must stay short enough to release the shared worker; an elapsed-time wait or asynchronous dependency must not hold that worker. SerialTaskRunner provides that execution policy while concrete work implements YieldingTask.

YieldingTask.runStep()
        |
        v
    TaskStep
 /      |       |       \
AGAIN AFTER(t) AWAIT(c) DONE
  |      |       |       |
  |      |       |       +--> complete this run
  |      |       +----------> completion callback; later re-admit
  |      +------------------> JDK timer; later re-admit
  +-------------------------> submit next step at executor queue back

SerialTaskRunner owns runner-local bounded pending-step admission plus a reference to the Runtime-owned single-thread ScheduledExecutorService. One submitted TaskRun step executes exactly one runStep(). AGAIN submits the same run's next step at the executor queue back. AFTER(delay) uses the JDK scheduler as a timer and submits the next step only after the delay. AWAIT(completion) registers an asynchronous completion callback and submits the next step only when that dependency finishes. DONE completes the run.

There is no task-specific serial-lane layer between a cooperative task and the JDK scheduler. Delays and asynchronous waits control when a TaskRun becomes eligible again and consume no runner pending-step slot while waiting.

AbstractTask is the reusable lifecycle owner for recurring state machines. A concrete task still owns its operation state; the base class only owns run/wake mechanics:

event/request/completion
        |
        v
 AbstractTask.wake(SerialTaskRunner)
        |
        +-- no run active ----> resetForRun() + SerialTaskRunner.runTask(...)
        |
        +-- run active -------> remember one pending wake

run completes
        |
        +-- success + wake pending --> start one fresh current-state run
        +-- otherwise ---------------> idle

Repeated wakes during one run therefore coalesce into one follow-up run. Cancellation drops the pending wake and cancels the current run. The concrete runStep() reads current state; event payloads are not replayed as an implicit queue of state-machine transitions.

The responsibilities are:

YieldingTask
  one cooperative step contract
  component/operation state remains in the concrete task

TaskStep
  continuation decision: AGAIN / AFTER(delay) / AWAIT(completion) / DONE

AbstractTask
  reusable run lifecycle, wake coalescing, cancellation and completion hook

SerialTaskRunner
  bounded cooperative pending-step admission directly on one JDK scheduler
  JDK-timer and asynchronous-completion continuation
  optional caller-side bounded wait support

SerialLane<T>
  one typed bounded FIFO, one fixed queue worker, batching and metrics

RuntimeExecutors
  physical role-executor creation, sharing and lifecycle

Antenna control is a concrete consumer. AntennaManager owns a reusable main AbstractTask plus reusable SelfTestTask, InventoryTask and AntennaShutdownTask. Inventory requests and child-task completions wake the main task; the later step derives the next transition from current manager/device state.

InventoryTask drives requested inventory state to applied device state and owns power preparation, initialization, direct-antenna start/stop and multiplex rotation:

InventoryTask
  POWER_ON
      |
      +-- AFTER(powerStabilization)
      v
  INITIALIZE
      |
      +-- AGAIN
      v
  START_DIRECT / START_GROUP
      |
      +-- AFTER(inventoryInterval) when multiplexing
      v
  SWITCH / DONE

Each TimingSystemConductor owns a MainTask extends AbstractTask executed by its SerialTaskRunner. TimingNode.PROPERTIES.CHANGED only wakes that task. The later run reads every TimingNode's current functional state, derives inventoryRequired = any node OPEN, and calls the optional AntennaManager.setInventoryRequired(boolean).

The call records desired inventory state without waiting for hardware. Repeating the same value is idempotent and does not become an implicit retry. Explicit repeated engineering requests remain separate retry attempts owned by AntennaManager.

The cooperative model is optional. A component that only needs typed FIFO item processing uses a normal SerialLane<T>. A TimingNode Data Lane is such a lane. Its Task Lane uses SerialTaskRunner because startup and upstream work can yield or await another lane. Delayed/cooperative capability is composed only where it has a concrete responsibility.

A device/provider implementation may itself use the same pattern when its protocol requires multiple commands, waits or retries. That state machine remains inside the device boundary. No parent may block a shared worker while waiting for work that still requires that worker or the same serial lane.

This model realizes the SSD requirement for component-local ordered execution with a small, measurement-driven number of physical workers. It does not change component ownership or add parallel execution within one serial lane.

docs.title: DD-DependencyPlacement — Contract and internal dependency placement
docs.text:
Type: Detailed Design Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed placement rules for semantic contracts, implementation dependencies and the allowed direction between SI-01 packages.

Place contracts with the responsibility that owns their meaning:

presentation
  functional client interfaces / transport mapping / wire messages

application
  commands, queries, application-level ports and authoritative running
  configuration semantics

domain / shared semantic artifacts
  domain model, semantic ports, TimingData and UpstreamData contracts/representation codecs

io
  hardware, messaging and storage adapters

infra
  concrete cross-cutting technical support, including logging, diagnostics,
  configuration mapping and extension discovery

runtime
  concrete application composition, top-level running application and lifecycle

platform
  small JDK-only reusable primitives and execution-environment abstractions,
  including serial execution and local typed events

Do not create one generic top-level api package merely to collect interfaces.

docs.title: Internal dependency direction
docs.text:
presentation --> application
application  --> domain / I/O / platform
domain       --> I/O / shared infra support / platform
io           --> platform / JDK
runtime      --> application / domain / presentation / I/O / infra / platform
infra        --> owned support contracts + platform / JDK / selected support libraries
platform     --> JDK and low-level environment only

The normal dependency direction follows the layer order and is intentionally easy to read from imports. I/O code does not import Application or Domain merely to reverse a dependency. Domain may call an I/O component directly when the domain behaviour requires it. In the current design, domain.system.TimingSystemConductor calls the optional AntennaManager through its semantic desired-inventory API. TimingSystem owns that composition relationship; AntennaManager retains all device mechanics and never depends on Domain.

For example:

LogBook
  -> TimingDataPersistence
       -> AppendOnlyRecordStore
            <- FileAppendOnlyRecordStore selected by Runtime

Dependency direction is intentionally one-way:

upstream / presentation / post-processing
          |
          v
LogBookAccessor
          ^
          |
LogBook
  ├── LogBookDataLane -> SerialLane
  ├── LogBookOperations -> LogBookState + TimingDataPersistence
  ├── LogBookStatus -> published CURRENT Status
  └── LogBookState -> LogBookData

domain.node.logbook must not import domain.node.upstream. A deployment that only commits/persists LogBookData therefore does not require an upstream component.

The typed upstream boundaries mirror lane ownership rather than exposing mutable collaborators:

  • LogBookAccessor is the single intentional LogBook contract for both internal and external consumers. execute(command) submits a command without a caller result; process(command) and process(query) return a result. Query processing may use CURRENT or ORDERED consistency without changing that public result-bearing contract. LogBookSync processes timingDataHead() and timingDataRange(...) through LogBookQuery; mutable LogBookData remains Data Lane-owned.
  • RaceDataState validates a RACE_DATA change set against copies and installs TeamAssignments and StageStartTimes atomically on the Task Lane. The containing DN_PACKET is confirmed with RECV only after that successful Task Lane application; no Data Lane hop is required for RaceData. LogBook publishes LogBookStatus.LOADED after persisted TimingData has loaded and LogBookStatus.ERROR after load failure. NodeService.MainTask handles only that status. NodeState owns DataTask, which then chooses its own bounded timingDataRange(...) reads and yields between those reads while rebuilding Task Lane-owned active-WP state. Each later successful commit publishes only that committed TimingData record as a wake signal for DataTask. This is a data dependency, not a Task Lane lifecycle dependency.

LogBookData remains passive and owns no event. This is deliberate: only LogBook knows that persistence succeeded and LogBookData visibility has crossed the commit boundary. Consumers such as upstream delivery, post-processing or presentation subscribe outward from that data boundary. Neither lane synchronously waits for work queued on the other lane.

AppendOnlyRecordStore contains only opaque-record storage semantics. DefaultTimingDataPersistence owns TimingData codec, TimingNodeId and sequence validation. This keeps io.storage independent from Domain. Executable composition may depend on the complete supported application-core surface and selected external libraries.

No traceability relationships are recorded for this object.

docs.title: DD-DomainIntegration — Domain data and upstream composition
docs.text:
Type: Detailed Design Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Domain composition for LogBook/TimingData ownership, shared UpstreamData semantics and routing boundaries.

TimingNode owns its active LogBook and node state. TimingSystem additionally owns one Upstream component with one NodeUpstream per TimingNode.

UpstreamData carries one semantic message inside an UP_PACKET or DN_PACKET. Current messages include RaceData, TimingData, TIMING_DATA_REQ, SEQ, RECV and PING. The packet carries packetNr independently from the semantic payload. NodeUpstream owns the UpstreamData codec and is the first component that turns an encoded packet into that semantic hierarchy.

Generic Messaging resolves routing once at its transport ingress. A connector supplies NodeId + encodedMessage to the gateway's explicit ConnectorPort. UpstreamGateway uses NodeId to choose one fixed node-scoped UpstreamStream application port and does not inspect the encoded payload.

The resulting UpstreamStream owns that fixed application binding. NodeUpstream reads and sends encoded messages directly through the stream without passing NodeId back to the gateway on every operation. CONNECTED and DATA_AVAILABLE are typed local events carrying the producing stream object itself. Connector CONNECTED/DISCONNECTED facts use the same subject/observer pattern.

Engineering-specific IF-03/IF-06 adaptation lives below io.messaging.engineering: UpstreamApiMessage extracts the IF-06 NodeId needed for connector-to-gateway routing while preserving the complete encoded message. EngineerApiConnector owns the WebSocket session and bounded transport delivery only. Heartbeat cadence remains part of NodeUpstream's IF-06 protocol behavior.

A connector may be a full-duplex Engineering WebSocket or a RabbitMQ transport with asymmetric consumer/publisher resources; that difference is hidden below UpstreamStream.

NodeUpstream preserves semantic message order and delegates node-state mutation through NodeService. TimingData replay uses LogBookAccessor asynchronously and never exposes mutable LogBook state. Send/retry/session mechanics remain outside node data transactions.

docs.title: DD-EventTagProcessing — EventData and TagProcessor realization
docs.text:
Type: Detailed Design Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Java realization of EventData-backed tag resolution, TagProcessor filtering/passage state and the boundary into TimingNode registration work.

The Java design consumes the shared event-data capability beside the shared TimingData capability. EventData owns the stable event-profile identity relationships needed to resolve TagId, RegistrationId and TeamId. The top-level TimingApplicationRuntime.create(...) API does not accept loose tag or team mapper dependencies.

The default/reference profile performs normal identity translation algorithmically rather than materialising thousands of map entries:

  • TT-A-NNNN-1 and TT-A-NNNN-2 resolve to RT-A-NNNN;
  • TT-R-NNNN-1 and TT-R-NNNN-2 resolve to RT-R-NNNN;
  • RT-A-NNNN resolves to TeamId NNNN;
  • reserve RT-R-NNNN resolves to TeamId only when reserve-assignment data is available;
  • NNNN is 0001 through 9999; 0000 is invalid.

The generic EventData API continues to expose semantic values rather than making TagProcessor understand this concrete string format. The intended shared API shape is:

RegistrationId registrationIdFor(TagId tagId)
List<TagId> tagIdsFor(RegistrationId registrationId)
TeamId teamIdFor(RegistrationId registrationId)
RegistrationId registrationIdFor(TeamId teamId)

A missing stable mapping is represented explicitly by the API contract. In the default/reference profile, normal RegistrationId/TeamId conversion is algorithmic while reserve RegistrationId/TeamId conversion has no stable EventData answer until assignment data exists. Runtime TeamId resolution may layer TimingNode TeamAssignments on top of EventData without changing TagProcessor's TagId-to-RegistrationId responsibility.

The provider/antenna implementation may decode or decrypt proprietary source bytes, but after that boundary generic code uses the shared eventdata.TagId. TagObservation therefore carries TagId, RSSI, absolute UTC epoch milliseconds and process-local monotonic nanoseconds. The absolute value may later become TimingData; the monotonic value is used only for elapsed passage rules. Generic tag processing does not reconstruct a TimingTimestamp wrapper.

TagProcessor resolves each observation through EventData and keeps its TagObservationFilter keyed by RegistrationId. The existing registration-keyed filtering model is retained rather than creating independent per-tag filters.

The burst/passsage state is extended with per-TagId statistics and the selected observation identity. A package-level immutable diagnostic snapshot exposes this state read-only for Presentation/engineering use. The snapshot is diagnostic; it is not persisted as TimingData and cannot mutate TagProcessor state.

The duplicate filter remains keyed by RegistrationId. Once TimingNode accepts a registration, every TagId resolving to that RegistrationId is suppressed by the same duplicate window.

RACE_DATA is semantic Central-owned current-state input, not a mutable domain object and not a historical source-sequenced stream. Its incremental changes are applied on the Task Lane to passive state such as TeamAssignments and StageStartTimes. EventData remains the owner of stable TagId/RegistrationId/TeamId profile semantics; TeamAssignments owns only live RegistrationId-to-TeamId overrides where EventData has no stable TeamId.

TimingNode remains the visible Domain component boundary used by higher layers, but it is a composition/lifecycle facade rather than a queue implementation. It composes LogBook, NodeService, its node-local TagProcessor and one SerialTaskRunner.

LogBook owns Data Lane command/query execution, durable TimingData commit, load status and post-commit publication. Normal Data Lane items use TimingNodeDataLane -> SerialLane<TimingNodeDataItem>. Persisted-data loading is not a Data Lane item: TimingNode.MainTask calls LogBook.loadPersistedData() as its startup step on the shared node worker.

NodeService owns Task Lane input processing, lifecycle and LogBook-status coordination. Its MainTask handles only LogBook availability. NodeState owns the retained live and derived node data and directly implements both the read-only NodeStateAccessor and the separate engineering/test NodeStateTestControl. Normal consumers receive only the read-only accessor; engineering composition receives the test control explicitly. DataTask owns bounded active-WP TimingData catch-up and StateQuery owns result-bearing ordered state reads. RaceDataState, ActiveRegistrations and RegisteredTeams keep their specialized data responsibilities behind NodeState rather than becoming fields on TimingNode. Other node-owned cooperative tasks use the same runner and therefore the same bounded TaskRun FIFO.

TagProcessor owns one SerialLane<TagObservation>. Runtime supplies the same single-thread ScheduledExecutorService both as that lane's backing executor and as the processor's direct timer/execution facility for policy changes, passage expiry and duplicate housekeeping. No second scheduled lane or observation queue is layered around it.

TimingNode itself owns functional OPEN/CLOSED state, current LocationId and its internal startup/execution readiness. A LogBook load failure remains LogBook health; it does not make the TimingNode execution path itself ERROR and does not replace functional state.

A production TimingNode is always constructed as a complete capability. TimingDataPersistence, TimingDataFactory, the injected absolute-time supplier, EventData/tag-processing configuration and both execution lanes are constructor dependencies; there is no lifecycle-only or partially configured production node. The only non-public construction seam exists for deterministic TimingNode execution-boundary tests and is documented as test-only in code.

TimingNode extends LifecycleComponent; the base class owns the generic active/inactive lifecycle fact. TimingNode therefore does not keep a second active field. Its protected activation hook first starts the node SerialTaskRunner, then uses ComponentLifecycleManager to activate NodeService, LogBook and TagProcessor. LogBook activation starts normal Data Lane admission; TagProcessor activation starts its observation SerialLane. TimingNode then admits MainTask and returns without waiting for persisted-data loading. No public TimingNode activate/deactivate API is exposed.

When a public component operation must reject an inactive lifecycle, the reusable failIfInactive() guard belongs to LifecycleComponent together with the active/inactive fact. A concrete component supplies the failure factory; TimingNode uses an ordinary IllegalStateException because inactive lifecycle is not a second domain-result state. The lifecycle package therefore remains independent from TimingNode-specific failure types.

Functional state is immediately available as CLOSED with no LocationId. Persisted TimingData loading runs asynchronously in TimingNode.MainTask on the shared node worker and rebuilds LogBookData outside the Data Lane item queue. Loading never defines or reconstructs functional OPEN/CLOSED state. A load failure remains LogBook health and does not by itself make the TimingNode execution path ERROR.

LogBook queries expose two explicit consistency modes:

CURRENT
  latest safely published completed snapshot; no lane queue/wait/timeout

ORDERED
  execute on the Data Lane after earlier queued LogBook work

The one-argument LogBook query remains ORDERED. A caller chooses CURRENT only when that LogBookQuery explicitly supports it. Status and the published LogBook head support CURRENT; count and record/range reads remain ORDERED. Task-owned state reads use NodeStateAccessor and execute on the NodeService Task Lane.

State-changing TimingData commands still execute on the Data Lane. After durable append and in-memory commit, LogBook publishes one immutable committed-TimingData fact through NEW_DATA_ENTRY.

TimingNode owns functional OPEN/CLOSED state and current LocationId as separate Property<T> values in one PropertyContainer. open() and close() set the typed properties and then call PropertyContainer.update(). The container compares against its previous baseline and publishes one PropertyUpdate containing all properties that changed in that logical update.

Lifecycle deactivation resets the transient values to CLOSED/no-location and calls PropertyContainer.sync(), so teardown does not emit a normal runtime state-change event. LogBook load/commit failures remain owned by LogBook/diagnostic behaviour and do not create a second TimingNode health-state model.

The runtime transition and lifecycle-record submission share the same short TimingNode state/admission lock used by automatic-registration admission. The transition is applied first, then the corresponding NODE_OPEN/NODE_CLOSE command is submitted to LogBook before the lock is released. A registration admitted before CLOSE is therefore already queued before NODE_CLOSE; a later registration sees CLOSED and is rejected. Antenna inventory may stop asynchronously after CLOSED without requiring a CLOSING state or a second registration-block flag.

TimingNode republishes LogBook NEW_DATA_ENTRY as the node-level TIMING_DATA_COMMITTED event, but that event reports only committed TimingData. Queue rejection or later NODE_OPEN/NODE_CLOSE record persistence failure does not reverse current functional TimingNode state. A direct LogBook lifecycle command or persisted TimingData load likewise does not mutate functional OPEN/CLOSED state or LocationId. LogBook owns committed TimingData and recovery state; TimingNode owns its separate functional runtime state.

State-changing process(command) remains non-reentrant: a command may not synchronously re-enter the same Data Lane behind itself. ORDERED queries are different. If the caller is already executing on the Data Lane, earlier queued work has already run before the current turn, so the query reads the ordered state directly without queueing or waiting again. CURRENT reads do not enter the lane. Bounded visitors remain short/non-blocking and must not start reentrant state-changing LogBook commands.

TimingNodeTypes is only a Java source-code grouping for TimingNode values: FunctionalState, the implementation-internal OperationalState, and the OpenResult / CloseResult values. It has no runtime state, lifecycle or architectural responsibility and therefore does not appear as another component in Figure SI01-01. LogBookStatus remains LogBook-owned and is not folded into TimingNodeTypes.OperationalState.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Java composition/lifecycle design for TimingApplicationRuntime, SimulationRuntime, PresentationRuntime and the built-in Console, RemoteShell and API adapters.

timing-point-app is the executable consumer of the application-core library.

Its executable package is deliberately thin:

oss.relay.timing.timingpoint.app/
  Main.java

The application core owns the reusable SI-01 runtime and supporting infrastructure:

oss.relay.timing/timingpoint/
  runtime/
    Lifecycle.java
    TimingApplicationRuntime.java
    RuntimeExecutors.java
    RuntimeTimeSources.java
    simulation/
      SimulationRuntime.java
      SimulatedTagScenarioRunner.java
    config/
      Config.java
      Presentation.java
      Api.java
      YamlLoader.java
  infra/
    BuildIdentity.java
    EmbeddedBuildIdentityLoader.java
    logging/
      Logging.java
      LoggingConfig.java
      LoggingLevel.java
      LoggingFileConfig.java
      LoggingControl.java
      TimestampedFileLogHandler.java
      CompactLogFormatter.java
    loggingserver/
      LoggingServer.java
      LoggingServerConfig.java
      LiveLogHandler.java

runtime/ owns knowledge of the concrete running application through TimingApplicationRuntime, execution-resource construction and the effective composition configuration. Figure SI01-01 shows this explicitly as the Runtime block. Runtime is not another business/domain layer; it is where the executable object graph is assembled.

The executable composition must remain readable as one linear construct-system-wire-start flow. Runtime constructs and resolves; the constructed TimingSystem fixes its own stable inter-component event graph before activation. The Runtime composition root constructs 1..N domain.system.TimingSystem components from validated effective configuration. Each TimingSystem contains 1..N TimingNodes and one TimingSystemConductor, and uses associated I/O components such as AntennaManager. Runtime resolves the concrete construction inputs and antenna-to-node mapping, then constructs the TimingSystem component.

validated effective configuration
  -> PlatformEnvironment / Runtime time / shared executors
  -> construct TimingNodes, AntennaManager and TimingSystemConductor
  -> construct domain.system.TimingSystem
       -> connect TimingNode status to TimingSystemConductor
       -> connect AntennaManager observations to TimingNode ingress
       -> connect UpstreamStream events to matching NodeUpstream inputs
  -> register TimingSystem with application.ApplicationConductor
  -> start physical workers
  -> application.ApplicationConductor.activate()   [application lifecycle boundary]
       -> ComponentLifecycleManager activates TimingSystem
            -> TimingSystem.onActivate()
                 -> ComponentLifecycleManager activates AntennaManager
                 -> ComponentLifecycleManager activates TimingSystemConductor
                      -> ComponentLifecycleManager activates TimingNode(s)
                           -> TimingNode.onActivate()
                                -> set node execution readiness INIT
                                -> start SerialTaskRunner
                                -> activate NodeService, LogBook and TagProcessor
                                     -> LogBook starts Data Lane admission
                                     -> TagProcessor starts SerialLane<TagObservation>
                                -> queue TimingNode.MainTask
                                -> return without waiting for persisted-data load
                      -> start system coordination SerialTaskRunner
                      -> wake first control run
  -> PresentationRuntime.activate()

TimingNode current state:
  -> functionalState starts CLOSED with no LocationId
  -> open()/close() update functionalState + LocationId directly
  -> NODE_OPEN/NODE_CLOSE TimingData records never drive current state
  -> persisted TimingData is not replayed to reconstruct functional state

TimingNode MainTask:
  -> run LogBook.loadPersistedData() synchronously on the shared node worker
  -> Data Lane items may be admitted meanwhile but cannot run on that same worker yet
  -> rebuild/publish LogBook recovery state and INITIAL_DATA_LOADED
  -> LogBook load failure remains a LogBook problem
  -> yield once so queued NodeService derived-state rebuild work can run
  -> mark the TimingNode execution path OK
  -> only a MainTask/execution failure marks TimingNode execution ERROR

system control run:
  -> read functionalState of every TimingNode directly
  -> calculate whether any node is OPEN
  -> call AntennaManager.setInventoryRequired(...)
  -> AntennaManager reconciles hardware asynchronously

Runtime owns object construction, mapping resolution and physical executor lifetime. It does not install stable inter-component event subscriptions itself. The domain.system.TimingSystem component contains its TimingNodes and TimingSystemConductor, uses its optional AntennaManager and system-owned Upstream, and fixes the system-level event connections before activation. Runtime prepares resolved construction and mapping data and registers the completed TimingSystem with ApplicationConductor. ApplicationConductor orchestrates activation, rollback and reverse deactivation across complete TimingSystems. TimingSystemConductor coordinates the TimingNodes and their Domain inventory decision.

TimingSystem composes the optional AntennaManager and supplies it to TimingSystemConductor. The Conductor uses only setInventoryRequired(boolean); it does not call power, initialize, start/stop inventory or multiplexing operations. AntennaManager may keep a private Setting<Boolean> for requested/applied state and retry revision bookkeeping, but that state is not a cross-component settings API. Runtime resolves the IF-11 io.devices.antennaManagers binding by timingSystemId; at most one manager is composed for each TimingSystem. The manager still owns antenna power, self-test, initialization, multiplexing, recovery and shutdown mechanics.

TimingSystemConductor uses its own SerialTaskRunner; all such logical lanes currently share the Runtime-owned timingSystemConductorExecutor. TimingSystem activates its AntennaManager before its TimingSystemConductor and deactivates them in reverse order. ApplicationConductor only orchestrates complete TimingSystems and does not need a coordination lane. TimingNode and TimingSystemConductor activation establish execution context and return without waiting for persisted TimingData loading. The TimingSystemConductor activation hook wakes the first normal reconciliation run. TimingNode functional state is already available as CLOSED/no-location while LogBook recovery may still be running. Recovery does not replace functional state and does not participate in the inventory calculation. Later committed TimingNode property changes emit PROPERTIES.CHANGED and wake another reconciliation; the later run still derives inventory only from current functional state.

Tag events, upstream stream events and individual antenna commands do not pass through either Conductor. Runtime resolves configured mappings as pure construction/composition data. The owning TimingSystem installs each observation event link to the target TimingNode component boundary; TimingNode then delegates the observation to its internal TagProcessor. External system composition never reaches directly into the node's TagProcessor. Targets must belong to the same TimingSystem and one antenna may fan out to multiple nodes.

The same ownership rule applies to upstream. Runtime constructs one NodeUpstream and one node-scoped UpstreamStream for each configured node. TimingSystem then installs the fixed stream event links to that NodeUpstream's ordinary input methods. Neither TimingNode nor NodeUpstream publishes a static composition-only EventInput for these system bindings.

antennaManager.tagObservedEvent(antennaId)
    .subscribe(timingNode::onTagObserved);

stream.CONNECTED
    .subscribe(ignored -> nodeUpstream.connectionAvailable());
stream.DATA_AVAILABLE
    .subscribe(ignored -> nodeUpstream.inputAvailable());

For current component properties, TimingNode uses the generic Property<T> + PropertyContainer mechanism. Functional state and LocationId are separate strongly typed properties. After the owner changes one or more values it calls PropertyContainer.update(); the container detects changed properties and emits one PropertyUpdate through its normal EventSource<PropertyUpdate>. Related values such as OPEN + LocationId therefore arrive in one update message.

Other semantic facts still use named EventSource ports such as TIMING_DATA_COMMITTED and NEW_DATA_ENTRY. Method-based event access remains only where an abstraction contract requires dispatch. The antenna boundary may still use tagObservedEvent(AntennaId) because the selected AntennaId determines the source instance. TagObservation remains the immutable event value and does not need an AntennaId field merely for routing because the configured source identity is already known at the subscription point.

runtime.simulation.SimulationRuntime is an explicit simulator composition entry point. It selects simulated installations/mappings through the same TimingApplicationRuntime.create(...) path; it does not introduce a simulated domain path or bypass TagProcessor/TimingNode.

The running application's configuration is not the same object as the startup YAML/runtime mapper DTO. Runtime owns the concrete ApplicationConfiguration tree because that tree describes the composed executable and its current effective settings. Infrastructure owns the reusable typed configuration-value mechanics. the Application layer owns the configuration query/update use-cases over that runtime tree and exposes only a narrow control interface toward Presentation. Domain, Presentation and I/O consumers do not receive writable access to the runtime tree merely because they need one configured value.

The executable artifact remains deliberately thin. Its launcher/input adapter stays under ...eventtiming.app; reusable logging remains Infrastructure support. Main selects the config file, supplies process console streams and installs the JVM shutdown hook, but does not construct or order concrete Presentation adapters. Runtime composition owns PresentationRuntime, which creates the configured HTTP/WebSocket/remote-shell/local-console adapters and participates in normal activate/deactivate ordering. The IF-11 YAML mapper stays with runtime.config because it knows the concrete runtime configuration schema.

timing-point-core.jar
  oss.relay.timing.timingpoint.infra/
    BuildIdentity.java
    EmbeddedBuildIdentityLoader.java
    configuration/
      ReadOnlyConfiguration.java
      DynamicConfiguration.java
      ConfigurationChange.java
      ConfigurationUpdateResult.java
      DefaultDynamicConfiguration.java
      FixedConfiguration.java
    property/
      Property.java
      PropertyContainer.java
      PropertyUpdate.java

  oss.relay.timing.timingpoint.application/
    ApplicationConductor.java
    ConfigurationControl.java

  oss.relay.timing.timingpoint.domain.system/
    TimingSystem.java
    TimingSystemConductor.java

  oss.relay.timing.timingpoint.runtime/
    TimingApplicationRuntime.java
    RuntimeExecutors.java
    RuntimeTimeSources.java
    PresentationRuntime.java
    ShutdownSignal.java
    simulation/
      SimulationRuntime.java
      SimulatedTagScenarioRunner.java
    configuration/
      ApplicationConfiguration.java
      TimingNodeConfiguration.java
    config/
      Config.java
      Presentation.java
      Api.java
      YamlLoader.java

timing-point-app.jar
  oss.relay.timing.timingpoint.app/
    Main.java

timing-point-core.jar contains the JUL-based default logging infrastructure but still does not select an SLF4J provider. Provider selection remains an executable-composition concern: the default app contributes slf4j-jdk14 at runtime, while another consumer may choose another compatible composition and omit the default Logging component.

The executable startup/configuration flow is:

main()
  -> core EmbeddedBuildIdentityLoader
       -> executable-provided filtered build resource
  -> configuration resolution
       -> selected built-in application-profile defaults
       -> selected platform defaults
       -> selected operating-mode defaults
       -> explicit IF-11 YAML deployment overrides
       -> secret resolution
       -> validated effective startup runtime Config
  -> core runtime configuration-tree resolution
       -> compiled component defaults
       -> apply resolved IF-11 startup overrides
       -> create runtime ApplicationConfiguration tree
  -> Logging
       -> configure JUL level + console/file handlers
  -> optional LoggingServer
       -> attach live handler + diagnostics listener
       -> use Logging for current level / common formatting
  -> core runtime.TimingApplicationRuntime.create(...)
       -> create PlatformEnvironment
       -> create RuntimeExecutors and RuntimeTimeSources
       -> create one TimeSource for the current timing context
       -> construct reusable application/domain/I/O objects
       -> construct and wire each domain.system.TimingSystemConductor
       -> construct application.ApplicationConductor for application lifecycle
       -> construct configured PresentationRuntime adapters
       -> return composed TimingApplicationRuntime
  -> TimingApplicationRuntime.activate()
       -> RuntimeExecutors.start()
       -> application.ApplicationConductor.activate()   [root boundary]
            -> ComponentLifecycleManager activates TimingSystem
                 -> TimingSystem.onActivate()
                      -> ComponentLifecycleManager activates AntennaManager
                      -> ComponentLifecycleManager activates TimingSystemConductor
                           -> ComponentLifecycleManager activates TimingNode(s)
       -> PresentationRuntime.activate()
  -> executable waits for shutdown request and owns JVM shutdown-hook handling

The current runtime.config.YamlLoader implements only the explicit YAML subset already needed by the running application. runtime.config.Config is a startup/composition input and is not the authoritative mutable configuration object of the running process. Profile/platform/mode resolution is part of the configuration architecture but is not yet implemented; the architecture does not require a new public Java type for each source before that behaviour is implemented.

BuildIdentity and runtime Config are different inputs. Build identity is artifact provenance; application configuration is deployment composition defined by IF-11. The executable embeds deterministic provenance fields (application, version, exact revision, sourceRef, buildOrigin, dirty, apiVersion). Wall-clock build time, CI run/build id and actor/user are not embedded because they are per-run metadata rather than stable build inputs/context.

Reusable application behaviour should not migrate into the executable merely because the architectural responsibility is called application. When a reusable application-core runtime object becomes justified by real shared behaviour, executables should compose that object rather than extend a BaseApplication hierarchy.

The application core uses one explicit runtime composition boundary. There is no builder layered on top of another bootstrap object. runtime.TimingApplicationRuntime.create(...) constructs and wires the current graph. Runtime owns composition, physical execution resources and outer Presentation lifecycle. application.ApplicationConductor owns application-component lifecycle order. Each domain.system.TimingSystemConductor owns the TimingNodes and coordinated operational behaviour of one TimingSystem.

docs.title: DD-ExtensionAndComposition — Extension and product composition
docs.text:
Type: Detailed Design Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed design for supported consumer topologies, Java-8 provider discovery, public/private composition, artifact extraction and dependency checks.

The application core is deliberately not tied to one executable topology. Plausible consumers include:

single-system application
multi-system / simulation application
public reference/test application
private/product application

These are consumer possibilities, not modules to create now.

docs.title: Java 8 extension/provider mechanism
docs.text:
A concrete public/private extension requirement now exists, so provider discovery is no longer merely an optional capability. Keep the mechanism narrow and composition-oriented.

The first V04 implementation slice covers only EventDataProvider and TimingDataProvider:

IF-11 provider ids
        |
        v
runtime.TimingApplicationRuntime.create(...)
        |
        v
infra.extension.ExtensionRegistry
        |
        +--> built-in EventDataProvider("reference")
        +--> built-in TimingDataProvider("reference")
        +--> ServiceLoader external EventDataProvider(s)
        +--> ServiceLoader external TimingDataProvider(s)
        |
        v
resolve configured ids
        |
        +--> EventData
        +--> TimingDataFactory + TimingDataCodec
        |
        v
normal application composition

infra.extension.ExtensionRegistry owns only typed provider registration, duplicate-id detection, discovery from a supplied ClassLoader and lookup by stable provider ID. It is not a generic Plugin API and it does not know TimingNode/Application behaviour.

The public built-in EventData and TimingData providers both use the IF-11 stable ID reference. TimingData therefore has a concrete DefaultTimingDataProvider beside the existing default factory/codec.

For the Java 8 baseline, an external provider JAR uses normal META-INF/services metadata. A caller may create a dedicated URLClassLoader for one or more provider JARs and pass that loader to ExtensionRegistry; the registry then uses standard ServiceLoader. The registry does not choose a filesystem extension directory, scan arbitrary folders, own hot reload/unload or own class-loader lifecycle. The exact external-JAR directory/layout and dependency-isolation policy therefore remain separate/open deployment decisions.

Each configured TimingSystem carries its own eventDataProvider and timingDataProvider selections. The reference IDs remain the compiled/default profile values when a deployment does not override them. Runtime resolves both provider IDs per TimingSystem before creating that system's TimingData persistence or TimingNodes. Unknown configured IDs and duplicate discovered IDs within one provider family fail before normal composition rather than silently falling back.

A synthetic V04 test creates an external provider JAR and a dedicated URLClassLoader to prove that ServiceLoader discovery works outside the built-in class set.

Provider contracts belong with the capability whose meaning they create; class-loader/discovery mechanics belong under application-core Infrastructure support. Domain, Application and I/O component code must not depend on URLClassLoader, ServiceLoader or a generic extension interface.

Step 7 adds the typed UpstreamDataProvider family. Later slices may register AntennaProvider, CanProtocolProvider and DisplayProtocolProvider families in the same registry pattern when those capabilities are implemented. They are intentionally not created as empty families in the first EventData/TimingData slice.

IF-11 selects providers by stable provider ID. Missing providers, duplicate IDs or an incompatible provider/configuration combination fail during validation or startup rather than silently falling back to another implementation.

Whether the provider contracts eventually justify a separately versioned SPI artifact remains implementation/evidence-driven.

docs.title: Public/private composition
docs.text:
Expected private/product-specific areas may include:

  • production RFID control/protocol details;
  • product-specific I/O/protocol implementations;
  • production asset/source inventory and mappings;
  • production upstream schemas/codecs where sensitive;
  • deployment-specific composition/policies.

Prefer normal composition and constructor/factory injection. Do not introduce a subclass-based BaseApplication extension model. The provider mechanism above is the explicit runtime-extension boundary; do not generalise it into arbitrary plugin access from domain/application code.

docs.title: Artifact extraction criteria
docs.text:
Create additional artifacts only when a real boundary requires them. Candidate extractions include:

  • RabbitMQ/messaging I/O;
  • Linux/Raspberry-Pi platform support;
  • public/private RFID/CAN I/O implementations;
  • separately versioning event-timing-data if binary compatibility/release evidence requires an independent release cycle;
  • reusable test support.

Extraction is preferred over speculative libraries: keep package/responsibility boundaries clean enough that a proven boundary can be split without redesign.

docs.title: Architecture/dependency checks
docs.text:
Useful automated rules may include:

  • presentation packages do not own or persist application state;
  • Domain does not depend on Presentation; Domain-to-I/O dependencies must be explicit design relationships, such as domain.system.TimingSystemConductor -> AntennaManager;
  • platform packages do not depend on event-timing application/domain behaviour;
  • wire/protocol classes stay with their presentation or I/O capability;
  • semantic contracts are not moved into transport packages merely because transport code uses them;
  • public code contains no real deployment mappings or proprietary values;
  • domain/application/runtime components do not depend on extension class-loader mechanics;
  • duplicate provider IDs and unknown configured provider IDs fail deterministically;
  • the executable consumes timing-point-core rather than copying/forking application-core source;
  • the core artifact does not carry a concrete SLF4J provider/backend transitively;
  • an executable runtime contains exactly one intended SLF4J provider.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed composition of per-TimingSystem I/O ownership and the CanNetworkController / NetworkDeviceService boundary.

The I/O package structure is logical; executable composition is per TimingSystem. Hosting 1..N TimingSystems therefore normally constructs 1..N corresponding I/O compositions, each with its own configured Storage, Devices, Messaging and DeviceNetworks objects. Explicit lower-level multiplexing may share a physical resource, but the owning TimingSystem contexts stay separate.

CanNetworkController owns CAN-network lifecycle/discovery and CAN-device communication. NetworkDeviceService owns the general bidirectional network-device boundary. It may expose application data outward and accept device-originated messages/events inward.

The high-level architecture deliberately stops there. Service discovery, connection/listener/session handling and protocol framing are lower-level design concerns below NetworkDeviceService. Likewise, a smart-display/domain handler should not acquire socket, mDNS or transport knowledge merely because it is reached through this service. The smart display remains an external client and therefore does not require a Rev2WifiDisplay class inside SI-01 merely to mirror the hardware name.
