docs.title: DD-LoggingRuntime — Runtime logging infrastructure
docs.text:
Type: Detailed Design Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Java design for reusable Logging ownership, retained/live sinks, LoggingServer and runtime logging-level control. Generic level intent is defined by Java design rule DR-09; domain-specific TimingData/LogBook event-to-level choices are defined in SDD-01 rather than repeated in this infrastructure section.

Logging follows the same library-versus-executable composition boundary.

timing-point-core.jar
  -> slf4j-api only
  -> oss.relay.timing.timingpoint.infra.logging
       +-- Logging
       +-- LoggingConfig / LoggingLevel / LoggingFileConfig
       +-- LoggingControl
       +-- ConsoleHandler
       +-- TimestampedFileLogHandler + CompactLogFormatter
  -> oss.relay.timing.timingpoint.infra.loggingserver
       +-- LoggingServer
       +-- LoggingServerConfig
       +-- LiveLogHandler
       +-- client-initiated live diagnostics + temporary level control

timing-point-app.jar
  -> selects exactly one SLF4J provider
  -> default provider: slf4j-jdk14
  -> delegates SLF4J records to java.util.logging
  -> starts/stops core-provided Logging
  -> independently starts/stops optional LoggingServer

Execution model:

Domain / Application / I/O publisher thread
        |
        | SLF4J -> JUL LogRecord
        | snapshot + non-blocking offer
        v
bounded AsyncLogHandler queue
        |
        | one Infrastructure-owned writer
        v
tp-inf-logging
   +--> ConsoleHandler
   +--> TimestampedFileLogHandler
              |
              +--> BufferedOutputStream
              +--> periodic/batched flush

The default executable therefore never performs normal console or retained-file I/O on a TimingNode, TagProcessor, AntennaManager or Application coordination lane. Publisher-side work is limited to level filtering, creating/snapshotting the log record and bounded queue admission. Formatting and sink I/O happen on one daemon logging writer thread.

The queue is deliberately bounded. Normal publication never waits for queue space. When it is full, lower-severity records may be discarded; an incoming WARN/ERROR may replace one queued lower-severity record. Dropped records are counted and the writer emits a warning summary when it can deliver again. Diagnostic loss is preferable to applying hidden timing backpressure.

Accepted records preserve queue order. The retained file sink remains buffered and does not flush after every record. The logging writer flushes delegates periodically (baseline 250 ms), immediately after WARN/ERROR, and during shutdown. File rotation also flushes/closes the old generation. Logging.close() removes new publication, drains all records already accepted by the queue, flushes delegates and only then closes the retained file.

The baseline queue capacity is 4096 records. Queue capacity and flush interval are owned by LoggingConfig; the current executable uses the component defaults rather than adding IF-11 syntax prematurely. These values are implementation baselines and may later be made deployment-configurable if runtime characterization justifies it.

Local-console prompt redraw is also owned by the existing tp-inf-logging writer. ConsolePromptCoordinator is passive: console formatting records a 150 ms quiet-period deadline, and the logging writer shortens its bounded poll wait when that deadline is due. There is no dedicated prompt scheduler/thread. Repeated log records simply move the deadline forward, so one prompt is redrawn after the burst becomes quiet.

The optional LoggingServer remains separate. Its JUL handler performs only bounded in-memory admission; socket writes already execute on its own tp-inf-live-log-writer thread. It is therefore not routed through the retained console/file writer and a slow engineering client cannot block ordinary log publishers.

Working rules:

  • application-core code may compile against the SLF4J API but must not force a concrete provider/backend on consumers;
  • provider-neutral deployment values stay component-owned: LoggingConfig contains LoggingLevel and LoggingFileConfig; optional LoggingServerConfig belongs to LoggingServer; runtime Config may reference both as composition data;
  • the executable application chooses and configures the provider/backend before runtime.TimingApplicationRuntime.create(...) starts normal application composition;
  • the default Java-8 application uses slf4j-jdk14 so the provider delegates to JDK java.util.logging without introducing Logback;
  • concrete JUL backend/file lifecycle stays under timingpoint.infra.logging; the live diagnostics handler/socket lifecycle stays under timingpoint.infra.loggingserver; neither package defines domain/application contracts;
  • infra.logging must not depend on infra.loggingserver or runtime.config; the thin executable starts the two infrastructure components separately before handing control to runtime composition. infra.loggingserver may depend on the narrow public Logging runtime surface for current level control and record formatting, but the logging component does not construct or own the server;
  • LoggingServerConfig belongs to the LoggingServer component and carries its listener values (bindAddress, port); the default YAML loader maps the external logging.live syntax to that component-owned type;
  • LoggingLevel is a logging-domain value rather than LoggingConfig.Level, so live level control does not depend on an umbrella configuration class;
  • the core artifact owns that reusable implementation because it has no dependency on executable-specific YAML/resource loading and uses only JDK facilities plus component-owned logging configuration;
  • Logging is the primary runtime logging infrastructure component and owns backend setup, console/file handler composition, record formatting and the current global-level control;
  • LoggingServer is the separate externally reachable live-diagnostics component; it owns the live JUL handler plus logging-specific socket/protocol boundary, delegates temporary level changes to Logging, and is not a Presentation/IF-03 endpoint;
  • normal default console and retained-file output is dispatched through one bounded AsyncLogHandler; do not introduce per-component logging threads;
  • the retained file handler is a sink owned by the logging writer and must remain buffered between writer flushes; it must not flush on every application record;
  • queue overload is diagnostic loss, not control backpressure; the writer reports dropped-record summaries and prioritizes WARN/ERROR over queued lower-severity records when possible;
  • the default retained file sink uses the local wall-clock start/rotation timestamp as a human-readable filename, normally yyyyMMdd-HHmmss.txt; this timestamp is not treated as a unique or monotonic session identity;
  • Raspberry Pi startup must not assume that wall-clock time is already network-synchronised: the clock may repeat or move backwards across restarts, so retained log creation must use non-overwriting create semantics, add a collision suffix when necessary, and protect the active log from retention decisions regardless of timestamp ordering;
  • retained text records use the compact operator-facing form HH:mm:ss.SSS - [LEVEL] - message - [sourceClass.sourceMethod]; exception stack traces follow the record line when present;
  • LoggingControl owns the configured global level plus an optional temporary runtime override; applying an override changes the running logger threshold without mutating deployment configuration;
  • the optional diagnostic listener is a logging-specific engineering facility. The test client initiates its TCP connection, log delivery is best effort, and network failure must not be allowed to block ordinary log publishers;
  • the live diagnostics protocol is separate from the IF-03 status/event wire model;
  • another executable/private consumer may select another compatible provider without changing core/domain source;
  • exactly one provider should be present in a runtime composition;
  • provider/backend versions are pinned centrally by Maven dependency management rather than scattered through modules.

This keeps provider selection replaceable at the executable boundary while allowing the reusable application core to provide the default JUL logging infrastructure and its configuration contract.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Application-layer design for PresentationGateway and its node-scoped TimingNodeProxy boundary. Presentation transports remain outside this boundary. The application PresentationGateway is composed with the complete set of currently composed TimingNode instances. It creates one TimingNodeProxy per node, indexes those proxies by application-wide NodeId, and does not expose a separate single-node production mode. Presentation tests use complete test fixtures rather than a second construction path.

PresentationGateway is an Application-layer component named for the adjacent Presentation side whose traffic it mediates. Gateway names describe the side of the architectural boundary, not the owning package/layer. PresentationGateway is entirely in-process: external Console, shell, Web and API endpoints terminate at their Presentation adapters, and only those adapters carry external port notation in Figure SI01-01. UpstreamGateway follows the same directional naming principle on the I/O/upstream boundary, but owns external transport/integration rather than presentation-facing application operations.

Node-scoped presentation access is exposed through TimingNodeProxy. PresentationGateway owns application-wide presentation information such as build identity and capabilities; a proxy gives an adapter explicit TimingNode context for node status, commands, queries and events. The architectural composition contains one TimingNodeProxy per composed TimingNode (1..N). The default executable currently has one because the executable still composes one TimingNode. A proxy is an Application-layer boundary object, not a second owner of TimingNode state.

Functional state publication remains owned by TimingNode. LogBook publishes one committed TimingData fact after durable commit and publishes its failures separately. TimingNode republishes the committed data as TIMING_DATA_COMMITTED; NODE_OPEN/NODE_CLOSE TimingData records never drive functional state.

TimingNodeProxy.status() returns one client-facing TimingNodeStatus containing NodeId, LocationId and CLOSED/OPEN state. IF-03 maps those values directly to id, locId and state.

The Domain boundary stays small. TimingNode owns OPEN/CLOSED state and LocationId, exposes OPEN/CLOSE directly, exposes the LogBook through LogBookAccessor, and provides one synchronous processLocked(Supplier<R>) scope for application work that must stay ordered with OPEN/CLOSE. The Supplier runs on the caller thread while the TimingNode operation lock is held. The method does not queue work and is not a commit/rollback transaction.

Runtime composition supplies TimingNodeProxy with the shared immutable EventData, the node's NodeStateAccessor, the engineering-only NodeStateTestControl and LogBookAccessor directly. The proxy does not depend on NodeService, and neither TimingNode nor NodeService proxies EventData reference-data lookups. A team-based presentation command combines the current TimingNode.locationId() with EventData.registrationIdFor(locationId, teamId) at the application boundary.

State-sensitive presentation writes build the concrete typed LogBook command inside that locked scope so the OPEN check and current LocationId cannot change between the check and the ordered LogBook commit. Meaningful deferred work is named before it is passed to the boundary:

Supplier<CommandResult> addRegistration = () -> {
    CommandResult result;
    if (node.functionalState() != FunctionalState.OPEN) {
        result = CommandResult.nodeNotOpen();
    } else {
        LogBookCommand<TimingData> command =
                LogBookCommands.commitManualRegistration(
                        node.locationId(),
                        registrationId,
                        time,
                        timeSource);
        TimingData timingData = logBook.process(command);
        result = CommandResult.committed(timingData);
    }
    return result;
};

CommandResult result =
        node.processLocked(addRegistration);

A revocation already carries the original LocationId and registration values supplied by the interpreting layer. It therefore does not gain an OPEN requirement or substitute the current LocationId. It still uses the same processLocked(...) scope so presentation-triggered LogBook writes do not overlap an OPEN/CLOSE operation. This keeps TimingNode compact when more append-only ADD/REV record families are introduced; the node does not need one public method per TimingData record type.

LogBook reads remain direct through LogBookAccessor. They do not need the TimingNode operation lock merely because they read history:

LogBookAccessor logBook = node.logBook();

LogBookStatus status = logBook.status();

Presentation adapters use the node-scoped Application boundary:

TimingNodeProxy node =
        presentationGateway.timingNode(nodeId);

node.open(locationId);
node.addManualRegistration(
        registrationId,
        time,
        ManualTimeSource.OPERATOR_ENTERED);
node.STATUS_CHANGED.subscribe(statusListener);
node.NEW_DATA_ENTRY.subscribe(timingDataListener);

process(command) is the result-bearing LogBook path: the caller waits for the processed domain result. execute(command) is the fire-and-forget LogBook path: it returns after the command is queued and deliberately does not wait for the later domain result. Because this path has no caller result, LogBook owns queue-rejection handling: it records the rejection as a LogBook diagnostic and does not push lane-specific RejectedExecutionException handling into TimingNode callers. RFID/TagProcessor-style ingress uses this form so a device callback cannot be held up by persistence, LogBook work or another queued TimingNode operation.

query(query, consistency) makes the read contract explicit. CURRENT returns a safely published immutable read model without entering the node lane; ORDERED executes after earlier queued node work on that lane. The one-argument query(query) preserves ORDERED semantics. Query definitions declare supported consistency modes, so mutable LogBook reads cannot accidentally be requested as CURRENT. An ORDERED query invoked from the Data Lane reads directly because its ordering requirement is already satisfied; callers outside the lane queue the query and wait for its ordered result. State-changing commands remain non-reentrant. Typed command/query objects are local operation descriptions, not another component, central dispatcher or generic message bus.

ApplicationId, internal TimingSystemId and functional TimingNodeId are separate Java identities. TimingSystemId distinguishes multiple hosted/simulated systems locally; it is not automatically serialized into TimingData or exposed as an upstream address.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed design for ApplicationConfiguration, reusable typed Configuration values and presentation-facing ConfigurationControl use-cases.

The configuration design has three deliberately separate ownership levels:

Infrastructure
  typed configuration-value mechanics

Runtime
  concrete ApplicationConfiguration tree for this executable

Application
  query/update use-cases over that tree

Infrastructure provides the reusable value contracts. They contain no knowledge of TimingNode, TagProcessor, YAML paths or API routes:

interface ReadOnlyConfiguration<T> {
    T startupValue();
    T currentValue();
    boolean overridden();
    EventSource<ConfigurationChange<T>> changes();
}

interface DynamicConfiguration<T> extends ReadOnlyConfiguration<T> {
    ConfigurationUpdateResult override(T value);
    ConfigurationUpdateResult clearOverride();
}

A successful update replaces one immutable typed value atomically and emits one typed ConfigurationChange<T>. Validation happens before replacement. NO_CHANGE does not emit a change. INVALID and RESTART_REQUIRED leave the current value unchanged.

Runtime owns ApplicationConfiguration and its concrete branches such as TimingNodeConfiguration. This is the authoritative configuration tree of the currently composed process. It is not a generic key/value map and it is not the external IF-11/YAML DTO.

IF-11 TimingData storage is resolved during Runtime configuration/composition. The single-TimingNode io.storage.timingData.path shorthand expands to one node binding; the multi-node io.storage.timingData.nodes form resolves each application-wide NodeId to exactly one validated filesystem path before TimingNode persistence is constructed. Runtime passes the resolved target to the existing persistence implementation; this does not introduce a generic storage registry or make storage part of TimingNode domain state.

Application owns ConfigurationControl: the use-case boundary for querying current configuration and requesting runtime changes. Runtime composition supplies the node-scoped DynamicConfiguration<TagProcessingPolicy> views when constructing this control; Presentation never receives those Infrastructure objects or the concrete ApplicationConfiguration tree directly.

ConfigurationControl returns Presentation-safe startup/current policy projections, runtime-mutability metadata and semantic APPLIED, NO_CHANGE, INVALID or RESTART_REQUIRED update outcomes. Partial TagProcessing SET requests are serialized by this control and are built from the current effective policy, so omitted fields retain the value from the preceding accepted update rather than reverting to startup defaults. An applied change emits one post-fact application Change event; no-change, invalid and restart-required requests do not emit that event.

Normal components receive only the narrow Infrastructure read-only view they need. For TagProcessor that value is immutable TagProcessingPolicy. A runtime update that changes observationQueueCapacity is rejected atomically as RESTART_REQUIRED; the dynamic duration/cadence subset is not partially applied. TagProcessor reads currentValue() when making policy decisions. Its change subscription is used only for mechanics that need explicit re-registration, such as replacing the fixed-delay housekeeping cadence.

Runtime composition creates the concrete configuration tree from compiled component defaults plus resolved IF-11 startup overrides. Clearing a runtime override restores the resolved startup value; restart reconstructs the tree from those startup sources.

The default IF-11 file syntax is YAML and its parser/mapping stays beside the effective runtime configuration model. runtime.config.YamlLoader maps external YAML into runtime.config.Config; it is not a generic Infrastructure YAML utility. As profile support is implemented, configuration support resolves built-in profile/platform/mode defaults plus explicit deployment YAML before runtime composition starts.

The resolver responsibility must remain data/composition oriented:

  • application profiles are data/default templates, not Java subclasses;
  • do not introduce profile-specific Application subclasses or a profile-specific domain hierarchy;
  • profile defaults may select topology/cardinality and capability defaults;
  • platform defaults may select environment-specific values;
  • operating-mode defaults may replace real providers with simulated providers;
  • explicit IF-11 deployment values have highest non-secret precedence;
  • runtime.TimingApplicationRuntime.create(...) consumes only the resolved/validated runtime Config and contains no profile-name switches.

SnakeYAML is therefore an application-core implementation dependency; the IF-11 contract remains independent of SnakeYAML APIs and another input adapter may construct the same typed effective runtime Config without YAML.

Build-identity interpretation is reusable for the same reason. The application core owns BuildIdentity and EmbeddedBuildIdentityLoader. The concrete executable still owns the filtered event-timing-build.properties resource and build-time provenance injection, because those values identify that executable artifact. The core loader only interprets the classpath resource and has no dependency on app.Main or another app class.

The implemented presentation structure is:

presentation/
  interfaces/
    console/
      LocalConsole
    shell/
      RemoteShellServer
    api/
      HttpEndpoint
      WebSocketEndpoint
      WebSocketOutboundDelivery
      MessageWriter
  common/
    terminal/
      TerminalSession

Console and remote shell are separate presentation interfaces. They share the line-oriented command parsing and text presentation in presentation.common.terminal.TerminalSession; both call the same PresentationGateway application boundary and shutdown callback. The current shared terminal command baseline is:

help
version
status
node [id]
open <locationId>
close
auto-reg <registrationId> <time>
config
config tag-processing set <field=value>...
config tag-processing clear
log
log T|D|I|W|E
quit
exit

These are Presentation commands, not a second Domain/Application semantic contract. Each terminal session has one selected TimingNode. node [id] shows or changes that selection; open, close and auto-reg delegate to the selected TimingNodeProxy. Configuration commands delegate to ConfigurationControl. log reads/changes the temporary global log level through LoggingLevelControl; the single-letter forms map to TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN and ERROR. LocalConsole and RemoteShell therefore cannot drift into separate implementations of node or configuration behaviour.

Console, Remote Shell and API are baseline Timing Point Application capabilities. Application profiles do not add/remove or redefine their command/status semantics. Concrete network listener bindings remain deployment configuration, so a listener may still be explicitly left unbound/disabled without creating another profile.

The functional API currently contains:

HttpEndpoint
  +-- GET  /api/v1/version
  +-- GET  /api/v1/status
  +-- GET  /api/v1/configuration
  +-- POST /api/v1/node/{nodeId}/configuration/tag-processing
                    |
                    +--> PresentationGateway
                           +--> TimingNodeProxy
                           +--> ConfigurationControl

WebSocketEndpoint
  +-- WS /api/v1/events
  +-- STATUS_SNAPSHOT on connect/reconnect
  +-- STATUS_CHANGED only for real status changes
  +-- TIMING_DATA_COMMITTED after committed TimingData
  +-- CONFIGURATION_CHANGED only after an applied runtime configuration change

MessageWriter owns the IF-03 wire/JSON representation shared by the Remote API HTTP and WebSocket transports. It is not application/control logic and therefore does not live in the application layer or in global presentation common code.

The local class names deliberately omit the Api prefix because the enclosing presentation.interfaces.api package already supplies that functional context. Endpoint is used rather than Server for the transport-facing classes; in particular, HttpServer is avoided because the implementation uses com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer internally.

The WebSocket transport uses Java-WebSocket 1.6.0 in the reusable application core and keeps the JDK HTTP transport unchanged rather than replacing both transports with a larger combined stack.

WebSocketOutboundDelivery owns only per-client transport backlog bookkeeping. WebSocketEndpoint still owns connection/event semantics. The delivery helper does not buffer event values itself: it counts sends while the Java-WebSocket connection still reports buffered data. After 32 such sends without an observed full drain, it refuses the next event and requests close code 1013. This bounds application-driven growth of the library's otherwise unbounded outbound queue without blocking, retrying or moving backpressure onto TimingNode. Reconnect recovery uses STATUS_SNAPSHOT plus LogBook queries.

WebSocketEndpoint sends the complete current IF-03 status for STATUS_SNAPSHOT and STATUS_CHANGED. Functional-status and operational-health events both trigger a new complete response. Building that response reads only the safely published current values exposed by TimingNodeProxy; it does not enter or wait on a Data Lane.

A browser-based engineering client, if added, should consume the API like any other external client. It does not require a separate SI-01 presentation.web package.

Manual inspection is provided by an independent development tool:

test-client/
  TestClientApplication      plain Java launcher
          |
          v
  TestClientFxApplication    JavaFX development view
          |
          +-- ApiClient          HTTP/JSON client
          +-- ApiEventClient       Java 17 WebSocket client
          +-- RemoteShellClient          A05 raw TCP shell client
          |
          v
        SI-01

test-client/ is a standalone Java-17 application and does not depend on timing-point-core or timing-point-app implementation code. It may, however, depend on the separately reusable event-timing-data artifact because TimingData codec/provider reuse is now a real cross-executable requirement. This preserves the external-client boundary while allowing SI-01 and the Development Client to exercise the exact same public or proprietary TimingData translator.

The Development Client remains development/test support rather than a product software item. Its desktop/runtime/workbench choices are owned by the Engineering Client environment and do not change SI-01 design authority.

The shared Presentation-facing application boundary remains small: PresentationGateway.version() returns build identity, PresentationGateway.timingNode(nodeId) resolves one node-scoped TimingNodeProxy, PresentationGateway.timingNodes() exposes the composed proxy set for application-wide status/event wiring, and PresentationGateway.configuration() returns the application-owned ConfigurationControl. A simulation-capable engineering composition may additionally provide the optional Application-layer SimulationControl; normal production composition does not gain a simulated-device dependency merely because IF-03 can expose engineering operations. The proxy obtains current node status through the TimingNode query/ownership boundary; the configuration control operates on Runtime-supplied typed configuration views. Presentation adapters therefore do not read node-owned fields or the concrete Runtime configuration tree directly.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Java design for Runtime-owned physical role executors and component-owned bounded logical lanes.

Project-owned SI-01 runtime threads use the diagnostic name form tp-<owner>-<role>[-<qualifier>]. The prefix makes Timing Point Application threads easy to separate from JDK, Maven/JGit and third-party library threads in a debugger, profiler or thread dump. The compact owner abbreviations used by the current runtime are pl (Presentation layer), dl (Domain layer), io (shared device/network I/O executor) and inf (Infrastructure). The executable entry thread uses the special compact name tp-main rather than a layer prefix.

Examples:

tp-main
tp-pl-console
tp-pl-remote-shell
tp-dl-node
tp-dl-tagproc
tp-dl-system-conductor
tp-io-shared
tp-inf-logging
tp-inf-live-log
tp-inf-live-log-writer

JDK and third-party threads keep their own names, for example an HTTP dispatcher or WebSocket library worker. Do not rename those merely to make a thread dump visually uniform.

NetBeans development Run/Debug starts SI-01 in a separate JVM through Maven exec:exec, not the in-process exec:java goal. The Maven process may therefore own its own main, ForkJoinPool, JGit and other build-tool threads, but those are not part of the Timing Point Application JVM or its runtime thread model.

The child JVM is launched with the application runtime classpath and the configured IF-11 application file. Debug launch adds the NetBeans JDWP listener address to that child JVM. On Windows the exec action enables long-classpath handling. The application uses its normal JVM entry point; Main.main() names that actual JVM main thread tp-main. Packaged java -jar startup follows the same application code path without any IDE-specific thread handoff or launcher workaround.

The two remaining project-owned Presentation threads are intentional blocking-I/O waits: tp-pl-console blocks on local terminal input and tp-pl-remote-shell blocks on ServerSocket.accept() / the active remote shell session. They are not combined onto one worker because either endpoint could then head-of-line block the other. In the Java 8 baseline, two mostly-idle blocking threads are simpler and safer than introducing a selector/ NIO state machine solely to reduce visible thread count.

Physical worker names describe the shared executor role, not one logical object that happens to submit work. A TimingNodeId therefore does not appear in the TimingNode or TagProcessor worker-thread name: one worker services the lanes for multiple nodes over its lifetime. Node identity remains available in lane/component diagnostics and metrics.

Threads owned by the JDK or external libraries keep their own names.

docs.title: Thread priority and execution roles
docs.text:
The execution design isolates latency-sensitive TagProcessor work from the shared Domain/application workers. Each configured node has an independent Data Lane and cooperative Task Lane; the physical worker count is a separate capacity decision. Persisted TimingData loading is a TimingNode MainTask step on the shared node worker, not a Data Lane item.

shared TagProcessor role worker
  -> SerialLane<TagObservation> per TimingNode
  -> direct scheduled filter/housekeeping callbacks on that same worker

shared TimingNode scheduled executor
  -> Data Lane per TimingNode: SerialLane<TimingNodeDataItem>
  -> Task Lane per TimingNode: SerialTaskRunner
  -> TimingNode MainTask recovery runs as Task Lane work

shared TimingSystemConductor scheduled executor
  -> one SerialTaskRunner per TimingSystemConductor

shared I/O scheduled executor
  -> one SerialTaskRunner per AntennaManager
  -> bounded I/O/simulation work as composed

These logical queues/tasks may share a small fixed set of workers. A separate Task Lane does not make blocked persistence on a single worker run concurrently with a heartbeat. V01 measures physical worker demand.

Step 5 still starts with normal/default Java thread priority for all roles. D04 defines functional separation and makes later role-specific tuning possible, but does not assign numeric Java priority values.

V01 measures queue wait, execution latency, CPU/thread behaviour and fairness. The current reference stress workload is 20 registrations per second for the whole SI-01 application. That target is aggregate across all configured TimingNodes: adding a second node does not turn it into 40 registrations/s. Multi-node characterization should vary the distribution of that same total load (for example 20/0 and 10/10) to expose unfair scheduling or queue growth without silently multiplying the hardware requirement.

If evidence shows useful separation under load, role-specific priorities may then be tested, for example TagProcessor above TimingNode and background work below it. The exact values must be qualified on both the development host and the Raspberry Pi target.

Correct registration behaviour, ordering and overload handling must never depend on Java thread priority. Java priority is only a scheduler hint and may behave differently between JVM/OS combinations.

docs.title: DD-RuntimeWorkAndMeasurements — Registration workload and runtime measurement
docs.text:
Type: Detailed Design Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed execution-budget and measurement design for registration work, background/runtime work, counters, snapshots and engineering access.

The normal automatic-registration flow is:

antenna/provider callback
  -> Event<TagObservation>
  -> TagProcessor
  -> TimingNode.onNewRegistration(...)
  -> LogBook.execute(...)
  -> Data Lane worker
  -> TimingDataPersistence.append(...)
  -> LogBookData.add(...)
  -> timingDataCommittedEvent.emit(...)

The callback/queueing steps must stay short and must not write files, send network data or wait for presentation/upstream work. LogBook.execute(...) is the fire-and-forget boundary: it only tries to place the command on the bounded Data Lane queue and returns without executing or waiting for that command. The Data Lane processes queued work independently afterwards.

The Data Lane worker is allowed to wait for the required TimingDataPersistence.append(...) call because that local durable write is part of the TimingData commit. After the record has been written and added to LogBook, short local post-commit listeners may run synchronously on the Data Lane worker.

A post-commit listener that needs socket I/O, retry, upstream delivery or another potentially slow operation must hand that work to its own bounded delivery mechanism and return. Synchronous Event<T> delivery is therefore allowed; Step-5 measurements check whether listener execution time materially increases TimingNode queue wait or queue high-water.

Raw antenna-observation logging is diagnostic work. It uses its own bounded buffer and does not sit between TagProcessor and LogBook.execute(...). Losing raw diagnostic records does not change whether a TimingData registration is accepted or committed.

docs.title: Internal runtime measurements
docs.text:
Runtime measurements are engineering data used to characterize the running Java design. They are not TimingData, TimingNode domain state, application status or presentation/API data.

The registration path records only small primitive counters and monotonic durations at the component where the work happens. Reading measurements is a separate pull operation. A read may allocate an immutable snapshot because it is not performed for every observation or registration.

Three snapshot groups are used:

TimingNodeRuntimeSnapshot
  queue depth / high-water
  admitted / full / not-running / completed work
  total + maximum queue wait
  total + maximum serial execution time
  TimingData append attempts / failures
  total + maximum append time
  committed TimingData count
  post-commit event deliveries / listener failures
  total + maximum post-commit event delivery time

TagProcessingMetrics.Snapshot
  received observations
  observation-input queue full / processor-not-running ingress
  closed observation bursts
  mapped / unmapped observations
  registration duplicates
  TimingNode admitted / full / not-running results

JvmRuntimeSnapshot
  heap used
  live thread count
  GC collection count
  GC collection time
  shared role-worker CPU time when the JVM exposes it

The exact Java value classes may group fields for readability, but these three meanings must remain separate. A JVM/process snapshot is not a TimingNode snapshot, and tag-processing counts are not TimingNode queue counts.

docs.title: Counter ownership
docs.text:
The component that performs the work owns the hot-path counter update:

  • ExecutionMetrics owns the common bounded-admission, queue-depth/high-water, queue-wait and execution-duration counters. Each execution primitive owns its own instance: SerialLane measures queued typed items, while SerialTaskRunner measures eligible cooperative task steps submitted to the JDK scheduler. AFTER/AWAIT waiting time is not queue wait because no task-runner step is pending then. TagProcessor reads the metrics of its SerialLane<TagObservation>; direct scheduled callbacks are not a second execution metric. Because a physical worker is Runtime-owned and may back multiple logical lanes/tasks, an execution snapshot does not claim exclusive worker CPU time;
  • the TimingNode commit path owns TimingData append/commit and post-commit event-delivery counters;
  • TagProcessingMetrics owns observation, burst, mapping, duplicate and TimingNode-queueing counters for domain.node.processing and exposes them through an immutable TagProcessingMetrics.Snapshot;
  • physical role-worker identity/CPU time and JVM/process values are read on demand from the supported JDK management APIs.

Do not copy these counters into a second continuously updated model merely to make them easier to display.

docs.title: Engineering access boundary
docs.text:
The current one-TimingNode characterization uses one explicit Java reader:

domain/node/processing/
  TagProcessingMetrics
    -> TagProcessingMetrics.Snapshot

runtime/measurement/
  RuntimeMeasurementReader
  TimingNodeRuntimeSnapshot
  JvmRuntimeSnapshot

RuntimeMeasurementReader is constructed only by engineering-harness composition. It reads the component-owned counters and creates/returns the immutable snapshots above. The tag-processing snapshot is the existing TagProcessingMetrics.Snapshot; D05 does not add a second wrapper with the same fields.

Its visible read shape is:

TimingNodeRuntimeSnapshot timingNode();
TagProcessingMetrics.Snapshot tagProcessing();
JvmRuntimeSnapshot jvm();

The normal public Domain component contract does not expose runtime measurements:

TimingNode
  open(...)
  close()
  functionalState()
  locationId()
  PROPERTIES.CHANGED
  TIMING_DATA_COMMITTED

  X runtimeMetrics()

TimingNodeTypes therefore contains only Domain state/result/problem/exception types; an engineering runtime snapshot is not a TimingNodeTypes member.

RuntimeMeasurementReader is not exposed through PresentationGateway, IF-03, the local console or the remote shell merely for characterization. T01 obtains it from engineering-harness composition that already depends directly on timing-point-core.

A02 may realize the reader's internal connection to TimingNode-owned counters with package-private readers or composition-retained measurement handles. For tag processing, composition may retain the same TagProcessingMetrics instance that it passes to TagProcessor. That mechanical choice must not add a public measurement method back to TimingNode, must not add measurement types to TimingNodeTypes, and must not make the reader a second owner of runtime state.

docs.title: Snapshot semantics
docs.text:
A snapshot is diagnostic, not transactional. Each field must be safe to read while the application runs, but fields do not have to represent one globally locked instant. The measurement path must not pause registration merely to make all counters change atomically together.

Counter and duration totals are cumulative for the lifetime of their owning component. The harness calculates workload deltas from a before/after pair instead of resetting product counters between runs. Current queue depth is a gauge; queue high-water is a lifetime maximum for that component instance.

Unsupported JVM measurements use an explicit unavailable value in the engineering snapshot. Measurement unavailability or snapshot creation failure must not change registration queueing or TimingData commit behaviour.

No continuous measurement thread is introduced. Timer/scheduler work used for TagProcessor burst expiry is unrelated to runtime measurement.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed Java design for the shared TimingData API, default profile, factory/codec boundary and typed provider mechanism.

Both SI-01 and the Development Client need common TimingData contracts without depending on the whole SI-01 application core. The shared artifact therefore owns the semantic interfaces and value types that every supported TimingData profile must implement; it does not require one concrete record class for all profiles.

The traced Java semantic model is intentionally small:

shared/timing-data
  TimingData
    common TimingNodeId / sequence / LocationId / time access
    AutomaticRegistration
      RegistrationId
    ManualRegistration
      RegistrationId
      ManualTimeSource
    ManualTimeSource
    RecordKey
  LocationId
  RegistrationId
  TimingTimestamp
  TimingDataFactory
    Context
  TimingDataCodec
    CodecException
  TimingDataProvider

default profile
  DefaultTimingDataFactory
    private automatic/manual immutable implementations
  DefaultTimingDataCodec

test / product-specific profile
  DummyEventTimingDataFactory
    private profile-specific immutable implementations
  DummyEventTimingDataCodec

There is no intermediate public RegistrationData interface. Automatic and manual registration are already the useful type-safe variants, so another level would add hierarchy without giving callers a stronger contract.

LocationId and RegistrationId are standalone shared value types because they are used at boundaries beyond one concrete TimingData subtype. They define stable Java/IF-05 representations and only minimal structural validity. Concrete event/profile/reference-data meaning and allowed values remain outside the shared library.

Likewise, TimingNodeStateData and RegistrationRevokedData are not created from old record-enum values. UC-002 still defers OPEN/CLOSE-as-TimingData and the current use-case baseline does not require revocation. Add those semantic types only after a promoted requirement justifies them.

The semantic interfaces are common. A configured profile supplies simple immutable implementing classes:

TimingData.AutomaticRegistration automatic =
        timingDataFactory.createAutomaticRegistration(context, registrationId);

TimingData.ManualRegistration manual =
        timingDataFactory.createManualRegistration(
                context, registrationId, TimingData.ManualTimeSource.OPERATOR_ENTERED);

The return types preserve variant type safety even when the configured provider returns a different concrete implementation.

docs.title: Stateless TimingData factory
docs.text:
TimingDataFactory is a stateless construction service. It does not validate TimingNode state policy, allocate sequence numbers, resolve TagId or TeamId, commit data, own a LogBook or publish events. Those responsibilities stay with the TimingNode and its contained domain components.

Source/reference resolution happens outside the TimingData factory. EventData owns TagId-to-RegistrationId and stable RegistrationId-to-TeamId relationships. Live TeamId lookup may fall back through TeamAssignments:

TagId -> EventData -> RegistrationId
                        |
                        +-> EventData stable TeamId
                        |
                        +-> TeamAssignments fallback TeamId

TimingData continues to store the already resolved RegistrationId; TeamId is derived for race/stage views and does not become TimingData identity.

The factory receives the already selected common construction values in one generic context and only the extra values required by the requested variant:

TimingData.AutomaticRegistration createAutomaticRegistration(
        TimingDataFactory.Context context,
        RegistrationId registrationId);

TimingData.ManualRegistration createManualRegistration(
        TimingDataFactory.Context context,
        RegistrationId registrationId,
        TimingData.ManualTimeSource timeSource);

TimingDataFactory.Context
  timingNodeId
  sequenceNumber
  locationId
  effectiveTime
  recordedAt

For the current manual variant, TimingData.ManualTimeSource is constrained to SYSTEM_ASSIGNED or OPERATOR_ENTERED. Automatic registration uses observed time by definition, so callers do not pass an origin or OBSERVED flag merely to restate the return type.

The context contains values only. It does not contain TimingNode, LogBook, stores, services or other mutable collaborators.

The design does not use an abstract TimingData base class. Concrete immutable implementations may delegate to TimingDataFactory.Context. Introduce a private/protected helper only when multiple real implementations show enough repeated behaviour to justify it; such a helper remains implementation reuse, not an additional public semantic layer.

docs.title: Provider boundary
docs.text:
A TimingDataProvider supplies a coherent family:

TimingDataProvider
  stable provider/profile id
  TimingDataFactory
  TimingDataCodec

The factory creates the concrete in-memory TimingData objects. The codec encodes/decodes the same profile family. The built-in default/reference codec uses Jackson's streaming API only; JSON Lines record framing, durable append and incomplete-tail recovery remain store responsibilities. Provider discovery and configuration remain bootstrap/infrastructure concerns.

A TimingDataCodec is a configured translator instance. Its per-record API remains deliberately small:

byte[] encode(TimingData data)
TimingData decode(byte[] encodedRecord)

Do not add event date, time zone, deployment configuration or UI context to those method calls. A provider that needs translation context receives and validates it at provider/codec creation time, and the returned codec captures the resolved immutable values it needs.

For example, a profile that serializes registration time as local time-of-day may capture an event-date/day-selection rule and a ZoneId or fixed ZoneOffset. If the profile cannot resolve a local time uniquely (for example a daylight-saving overlap) or cannot represent the semantic instant within its configured day scope, encode/decode fails according to that profile rather than guessing from the host clock.

This translation context is distinct from TimingDataFactory.Context. TimingDataFactory.Context contains semantic values of one record; provider configuration explains how those values are represented externally.

The current TimingDataProvider.createCodec() shape does not force a configuration mechanism by itself. When generic provider discovery/configuration is implemented, bootstrap must construct or configure the provider before asking it for a codec. If implementation evidence requires a typed provider creation/configuration object, that type belongs at the provider/bootstrap boundary, not in TimingDataCodec.encode/decode.

The provider therefore does more than representation translation, but it still does not own TimingNode business rules. It chooses the concrete TimingData implementation and its representation while preserving the common semantic contracts defined by IF-05.

Both the Java-8 SI-01 runtime and Java-17 Development Client can depend on event-timing-data. The Development Client may inspect the common interfaces without depending on SI-01 Domain classes. Profile-specific inspection can be added only where a real consumer needs it.

The current design keeps the default/reference profile inside the shared TimingData library while the design is still changing; do not create another production Maven artifact solely to mirror the conceptual profile split. A dummy event-specific implementation in tests is sufficient to prove that the common contract does not accidentally depend on the default concrete classes. A separate provider artifact becomes justified when a real independently deployed profile exists.

This artifact contains no SI-01 runtime/application classes and no JavaFX code. Its Java API must remain usable from both the Java-8 SI-01 baseline and the Java-17 Development Client.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed design for TimingNode ordered execution, durable TimingData commit, passive LogBookData reads and the local Event/EventSource publication boundary.

The Java design uses composition rather than an ActiveObject inheritance hierarchy. One TimingNode owns two logically independent bounded serial lanes:

TimingNode
  ├── PropertyContainer
  │     ├── functionalState -> transient CLOSED / OPEN
  │     ├── operationalState -> node execution INIT / OK / ERROR
  │     └── locationId -> current LocationId or none
  ├── Data Lane -> TimingNodeDataLane -> SerialLane<TimingNodeDataItem>
  │                └── LogBook
  │                     ├── LogBookDataLane -> result/wait/rejection mapping
  │                     ├── LogBookOperations -> commands, persistence, recovery + commit
  │                     └── LogBookState -> recovery state + LogBookData records
  └── Task Lane -> SerialTaskRunner
                   ├── TimingNode.MainTask -> startup LogBook recovery
                   └── NodeService
                        ├── MainTask -> LogBook INIT / LOADED / ERROR
                        └── NodeState -> retained live/derived state
                             ├── DataTask -> current head + bounded TimingData range reads
                             ├── StateQuery -> ordered result-bearing reads
                             ├── RaceDataState -> TeamAssignments + StageStartTimes
                             ├── ActiveRegistrations -> ordered registration list
                             └── RegisteredTeams -> unique team set / + - changes

The Data Lane is the sole writer for normal ordered LogBook commands and queries. TimingNodeDataLane adapts the generic SerialLane<TimingNodeDataItem> to typed LogBook-operation and upstream-turn items without creating another queue or thread model. LogBookDataLane owns result-bearing command/query completion and bounded wait mapping. LogBookOperations owns state-changing domain operations, TimingData creation, record-creation time capture, durable append, recovery reconstruction and commit metrics/logging. Internal registration commands carry absolute times as UTC epoch-millisecond long values; they do not retain TimingTimestamp wrappers. For the default IF-05 profile, effective time is canonicalized to the required 10 ms boundary before the TimingRecord is committed, while recordedAtMillis preserves the full 1 ms record-creation time required by recTime. LogBookState contains passive mutable state and committed in-memory TimingData.

Persisted TimingData loading is not a Data Lane item. After child activation starts normal Data Lane admission, TimingNode.MainTask calls LogBook.loadPersistedData() synchronously on the same physical node worker. Commands may queue during that load but cannot execute until the MainTask step releases the worker. A successful load publishes LogBookStatus.LOADED; load failure publishes LogBookStatus.ERROR. Status is directly readable and is not another Data Lane query. Each later successful commit publishes the committed TimingData record.

The Task Lane is the TimingNode's SerialTaskRunner. NodeService.MainTask handles only LogBook availability. NodeState groups the retained Task Lane-owned data while RaceDataState, ActiveRegistrations and RegisteredTeams keep their specialized internal responsibilities. NodeState directly implements NodeStateAccessor and NodeStateTestControl. Normal callers see the read-only accessor; engineering/test composition receives the mutation control separately, without an additional state-wrapper implementation object.

NodeState owns DataTask and StateQuery as execution helpers. DataTask owns the source cursor, bounded asynchronous LogBook reads and catch-up completion. It reads the current LogBook head and continues from its own nextSequence, fetching missing records with bounded ordered timingDataRange(...) queries through LogBookAccessor and yielding while each Data Lane read completes. StateQuery preserves Task Lane ordering for result-bearing reads and may first yield on DataTask catch-up. The current implementation reads at most 64 TimingData records per batch.

Later committed TimingData does not pass through NodeService or NodeState as a second history collection. The post-commit event only wakes DataTask; DataTask then catches up from the LogBook source. NodeState groups the current live and derived data but does not duplicate committed TimingData.

ActiveRegistrations stores one ordered compact scalar entry per committed registration ADD. TimingData is consumed at the input boundary and is not retained: the row keeps only sequence, effective epoch milliseconds, packed RegistrationId, numeric LocationId and validity. Its original sequence and WP are stable. A matching REV marks the newest matching valid ADD invalid rather than removing it from the display list; nonregistration records are ignored. Semantic TimingData value objects are reconstructed only for read/output boundaries. The display may visit all registrations for one WP in original source order, including invalid entries, and is responsible for tracking which rows it has shown. A bounded visitAfter(locationId, afterSequence, limit, visitor) pages through later ADD rows using the original registration sequence, avoiding repeated delivery of earlier rows. This cursor does not detect later revocations of earlier ADDs: the display also needs to revisit its already displayed rows to observe changed validity. Domain owns neither the display cursor nor a second per-display update index.

RegisteredTeams maintains the unique-team set of the currently open WP. The LocationId is scope of the whole projection rather than a key repeated in each retained row/map. Occurrence counts are still kept per RegistrationId so a live assignment change can move all existing occurrences to the newly resolved TeamId. The complete visitor supports the compact full synchronization burst; team order has no domain meaning and the CAN bitmap is independent of visitation order. Only post-rebuild zero-to-nonzero and nonzero-to-zero membership transitions produce incremental + / - notifications. Historical reconstruction itself is silent: the display first takes a full burst after the OPEN projection has caught up. CAN encoding, delivery and per-display synchronization state remain outside Domain.

Stage-start interpretation is split deliberately between ingress normalization and StageTiming. NodeService.applyRaceData(...) samples the shared TimeSource once and normalizes every IF-06 SET to one compact UTC long before it enters RaceDataState. A time-only value retains only UTC HHmmsscc and therefore remains below 100000000; a value that contains a date is stored as UTC yyyyMMddHHmmsscc. No missing date is added.

Absolute IF-06 values already define their UTC instant. Local date/time values use the configured TimeSource zone and reject ambiguous/nonexistent DST wall times. A time-only value uses only the zone offset active for the sampled timing context; the result remains time-only. If a variable-offset zone has a transition within the relevant twelve-hour window, the time-only value is rejected rather than guessing which offset applies.

StageTiming is the single elapsed/rollover rule. For a dated start it compares the explicit UTC date/time directly with the absolute registration passage. For a time-only start it evaluates same-UTC-day/previous-UTC-day rollover and accepts only the unique interpretation with 0 <= elapsed < 12 hours. Exactly twelve hours or otherwise unresolvable values remain known stage starts but do not produce elapsed time or rank.

The domain.node.registration package contains only active-WP registration-derived state. It is not a second history store. The LogBook remains authoritative for all LocationIds and all earlier OPEN/CLOSE periods.

While the TimingNode is CLOSED there is no usable registration projection. On OPEN(locationId), NodeState/DataTask clears the previous projection and scans the complete LogBook from sequence one in bounded batches. ActiveRegistrations admits only registration ADD/REV records whose LocationId equals the newly open WP. Therefore older registrations from earlier OPEN periods of the same WP return, while historical rows of every other WP are excluded. On CLOSE the derived projection is deactivated and cleared; reopening the same WP rebuilds it again from LogBook rather than relying on stale retained history.

Because LocationId scopes the whole active projection, an ActiveRegistrations.Registration row stores only sequence, effective time, packed RegistrationId and validity. Rows remain in original ADD sequence order. A matching REV searches newest-to-oldest and marks the newest still-valid row with the same RegistrationId and effective timestamp invalid; the row is not removed because a display may already have shown it.

RegisteredTeams is the second active-WP projection. It counts valid occurrences by RegistrationId and resolves those counts through current RaceData to one unique TeamId set. Repeated passages change only occurrence counts. A live assignment change can move all active occurrences for one RegistrationId. Historical replay after OPEN suppresses +/- events until DataTask has caught up; the full team visitor supplies the synchronization snapshot. Only later live zero-to-nonzero and nonzero-to-zero transitions publish incremental events.

Open/close requests may supersede a pending bounded LogBook read. DataTask therefore treats the requested LocationId as a generation: an obsolete partial batch is discarded, both projections are reset, and the newest requested WP restarts from sequence one. NodeStateAccessor reads wait for that reconstruction/catch-up before observing the projection. Its registration/team read methods take no LocationId because there is exactly one current OPEN scope.

These objects remain Task Lane-owned. CAN encoding, display cursor/synchronization state, persistence, elapsed-time result models and ranking calculations are outside this package.

Do not add a production query/result type merely because a unit or integration test would be easier to write with it. A new calculated view belongs in production only when an actual application, presentation or I/O consumer requires that behavior. Tests verify the retained state through the existing production boundary or package-local implementation tests rather than defining extra public API.

A failed persisted-data load leaves LogBook in LogBookStatus.ERROR with the concrete failure retained in LogBook diagnostics. The TimingNode MainTask still completes its own startup path to operational OK; TimingNode.ERROR is reserved for failure of the node's own startup/execution path. Neither condition replaces functional OPEN/CLOSED state or current LocationId.

RACE_DATA therefore does not cross to the Data Lane: packet duplicate detection, compact UTC stage-start normalization, transactional live-state mutation and downstream RECV completion happen on Task Lane task turns. TIMING_DATA_REQ/replay is different because its source is Data Lane-owned LogBookData; that path uses bounded asynchronous handoff and bounded TimingData batches. A cooperative task that needs a Data Lane query uses LogBookAccessor.submit(...) and TaskStep.await(...); it never blocks the shared worker waiting on that completion.

docs.title: Why composition instead of an ActiveObject base class
docs.text:
A reusable base class such as TimingNode extends ActiveObject<Work> is possible, but it would couple the domain type to one threading mechanism. Composition keeps that choice replaceable and lets the public TimingNode API stay synchronous and domain-oriented.

For state-dependent operations the caller uses the result-bearing LogBook path; device or callback ingress may use the fire-and-forget path:

final class TimingNode {
    private final LogBookAccessor logBook;

    LogBookAccessor logBook() {
        return logBook;
    }
}

TimingNodeTypes.OpenResult opened =
        node.logBook().process(LogBookCommands.open(locationId));

node.logBook().execute(
        LogBookCommands.addAutomaticRegistration(registrationId, time));

// LogBook is the Data Lane component boundary.
// LogBookDataLane owns LogBook-specific lane execution mechanics.
// LogBookOperations owns state-changing command/commit work.
// LogBookState owns passive state and committed TimingData; LogBookStatus owns published status.
// SerialTaskRunner owns cooperative TaskRun execution for the TimingNode Task Lane.
// NodeService.MainTask handles LogBook status and input-processing coordination.
// NodeState implements NodeStateAccessor and NodeStateTestControl; Runtime exposes them separately.
// DataTask rebuilds/catches up the OPEN-WP projection; StateQuery preserves ordered reads.
// ActiveRegistrations owns ordered ADD rows and validity for the currently open WP.
// RegisteredTeams owns the current open-WP unique-team set and live + / - changes.
// Calculated presentation/query models are added only for an actual production consumer.
// DownstreamDelivery invokes NodeService.applyRaceData(...) synchronously on the Task Lane
// before confirming the containing DN_PACKET.

The visible TimingNode delegates execution mechanics to its child components. execute(command) returns after queueing and has no synchronous domain result. process(command) and process(query) are the result-bearing boundary. An ORDERED query waits for its Data Lane turn; a CURRENT query may read an already safely published snapshot directly. The word process therefore denotes "handle this request and return its result", not "always enqueue this request". Callers use the intentional child boundary rather than reaching into mutable state.

The important split is:

open(locationId) / close / consistency-sensitive query
    -> queued internally
    -> execute against current ordered TimingNode state
    -> caller receives processed domain result

device/callback ingress that is explicitly offer-only
    -> bounded queue result
    -> callback may continue immediately
    -> later processing has no synchronous caller waiting for its domain result

A queue result is never used as a substitute for the domain result of a state-dependent command.

The Future used to connect the queued work with a waiting caller is an internal Active Object mechanism. It does not appear in the normal TimingNode application/domain interface. The current synchronous caller contract needs only an internal plain Future<R>; CompletionStage is not required.

Code already running on the Data Lane uses direct private/domain methods such as doOpen() rather than calling the blocking public open() method again. Re-entering a public blocking operation from the same serial lane would wait on work that cannot run until the current work item finishes.

docs.title: Operation results and execution failures
docs.text:
Keep normal semantic results small and owned by the boundary that defines them.

For example:

TimingNodeTypes
  FunctionalState
  OpenResult
  CloseResult

Application
  CommandResult
    COMMITTED
    NODE_NOT_OPEN

LogBook command result
  TimingData

CommandResult belongs to Application because it describes a presentation-triggered command, not TimingNode state and not a LogBook commit primitive. A LogBook registration/revocation command returns the committed TimingData directly. The proxy adds the normal application result around that value and decides NODE_NOT_OPEN before the LogBook is called.

Technical queue rejection, unavailable execution, interruption, timeout and execution failure are not another TimingNode result/state enum. The Data Lane retains the bounded wait guards and logs the concrete technical reason where it is known. The Java call aborts normal flow with an ordinary runtime failure. Forwarding Application/Presentation layers do not translate the internal failure taxonomy into a second public reason model.

A command wait timeout still has an important diagnostic distinction: already accepted work may complete later. The owning Data Lane log therefore records that the final command outcome may be unknown. An ordered-query timeout records only that no query result was obtained. That distinction belongs in retained diagnostics; it does not require a generic public operation-state exception.

Exceptions are not grouped into TimingNodeTypes. That source-only grouping is for actual TimingNode value/result types. Introduce an owner-specific exception only when callers genuinely need distinct programmatic recovery behaviour; otherwise ordinary Java runtime failure plus owning-boundary diagnostics is preferred.

The Java baseline uses separate wait guards for the two result-bearing LogBook operation families:

TimingData commit command
  OPEN / CLOSE / AUTO_REG / MAN_REG / REV
  default caller wait guard: 5000 ms

ORDERED LogBook query
  count/range reads that enter the Data Lane
  default caller wait guard: 2000 ms

CURRENT LogBook query
  published immutable/current snapshot
  no Data Lane wait timeout

The 5000 ms commit value is a guard on how long the synchronous caller waits for the complete ordered commit result. It includes time already queued ahead of the command plus command execution, durable append, in-memory commit and result delivery. It is not a statement that one file append is allowed to consume five seconds. Normal local persistence is expected to complete far faster; a timeout is an operational failure signal.

An accepted command is not cancelled when this caller wait expires. The Data Lane may still complete it later, so the caller-visible state-change outcome remains unknown until current state or a later committed fact establishes the result. An ORDERED-query timeout has different meaning: no query result was received within its wait guard, but no state-change outcome is implied.

These two defaults are explicit composition constants, not one generic operationTimeoutMillis. Runtime configuration is not added solely for tuning before target measurements justify it. Timeout log records include the effective duration so the value is observable when a guard fires.

docs.title: SerialLane design
docs.text:
SerialLane<T> is the generic bounded typed FIFO/one-worker primitive. It stores caller-owned values and receives an item processor at construction. The backing Executor sees only the lane's fixed queue-worker runnable.

The logical node topology is:

RuntimeExecutors.timingNodeExecutor
  ├─ TimingNode A Data Lane -> SerialLane<TimingNodeDataItem>
  ├─ TimingNode A Task Lane -> SerialTaskRunner
  ├─ TimingNode B Data Lane -> SerialLane<TimingNodeDataItem>
  └─ TimingNode B Task Lane -> SerialTaskRunner

offer(T) never waits for capacity and returns one of ACCEPTED, FULL or NOT_RUNNING. A successful first offer while idle schedules the one fixed worker. Further offers only extend the lane queue while that worker is scheduled/running.

One worker run processes at most maxItemsPerRun items that were available at the start of that run. If items remain afterwards, the same worker is scheduled once more. This creates a fairness point for sibling lanes sharing the same physical executor.

SerialLane does not define application exception policy, result futures or a FAILED lifecycle state. The item owner contains expected domain/runtime failures where required. A backing-executor RejectedExecutionException stops further admission and clears queued items because the lane can no longer guarantee execution. close() stops admission and waits for already accepted work to drain; it never shuts down the Runtime-owned executor.

Result-bearing domain adapters carry their own completion with the queued item. For example, LogBook query/command items complete their own CompletableFuture; the generic lane remains unaware of command/query semantics.

The required behaviour is:

  • queue capacity is visible and bounded per logical lane;
  • FIFO order is preserved per lane;
  • at most one worker for one lane is scheduled/running at a time;
  • one worker run processes no more than maxItemsPerRun items;
  • sibling lanes may share one physical worker and make progress at batch boundaries;
  • isExecutingOnCurrentThread() identifies ownership without exposing a lifecycle enum;
  • closing drains accepted work but does not own physical-executor shutdown;
  • Runtime stops physical role executors only after component lanes/runners have stopped.

ExecutionMetrics provides the shared queue/admission, depth/high-water, queue-wait and execution-duration model. Each SerialLane and SerialTaskRunner owns its own instance; metrics().snapshot() creates the immutable engineering view.

docs.title: SerialTaskRunner and direct JDK scheduling
docs.text:
SerialTaskRunner is an independent cooperative execution primitive. It does not subclass, contain or delegate to SerialLane; it owns runner-local bounded pending-step admission and uses the Runtime-supplied single-thread ScheduledExecutorService directly.

runTask(YieldingTask) creates one TaskRun and submits its first eligible step. Each executor turn invokes one runStep(). AGAIN submits the continuation at the executor queue back, AFTER uses ScheduledExecutorService.schedule(...) only as a timer, AWAIT attaches an asynchronous completion callback, and DONE completes the run. Delayed/awaiting tasks occupy neither a runner pending-step slot nor the physical worker until their continuation becomes eligible.

TagProcessor deliberately does not use SerialTaskRunner: observations are plain typed items, so one SerialLane<TagObservation> is sufficient. Its timed filter and housekeeping work runs directly on the same single-thread JDK scheduled executor that backs the observation lane.

Current composition is:

TimingNode
  -> Data Lane: SerialLane<TimingNodeDataItem>
  -> Task Lane: SerialTaskRunner
  -> TagProcessor: SerialLane<TagObservation>
                   + direct ScheduledExecutorService callbacks

TimingSystemConductor
  -> SerialTaskRunner
  -> shared timingSystemConductorExecutor

AntennaManager
  -> SerialTaskRunner
  -> sharedIoScheduledExecutor

SimulatedTagScenarioRunner uses the Runtime-owned sharedIoScheduledExecutor directly. It keeps at most 32 active scenarios and schedules only the next step of each scenario, so simulation work is bounded without another logical lane or scheduling wrapper. A lifecycle-generation guard prevents delayed work from a previous activation from emitting after deactivate/reactivate.

All execution is JDK-backed. Physical parallelism remains a Runtime decision; adding logical lanes or task runners does not imply adding threads.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Detailed composition of raw platform time and the shared semantic TimeSource used by Domain and I/O timestamp producers. The raw absolute wall clock and monotonic elapsed-time source come from PlatformEnvironment. Runtime composes a platform.time.TimeSource from the absolute Clock and passes that timing source to components that attach or interpret event time. TimeSource exposes both the absolute Instant and the configured civil-time ZoneId. The current baseline implementation is ClockTimeSource, which exposes the zone carried by its injected Clock; Runtime may therefore re-zone or replace that Clock without changing Domain consumers. Lightweight/custom TimeSource implementations default their civil-time zone explicitly to UTC.

TimeSource ownership is deliberately not encoded as TimingSystem or TimingNode API. Composition decides its sharing scope. The current single-node Runtime has one source; a later TimingSystem composition may pass one shared source to all TimingNodes and timestamp-producing I/O providers in that system. This preserves one corrected timing basis without creating another raw platform clock.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: EventData is a shared Domain capability parallel to TimingData. A configured EventData profile defines stable event-specific source/reference semantics, including the 1..N relationship between RegistrationId and TagId. SI-01 and engineering tools consume the common contract while an event-specific typed provider/profile library supplies the concrete profile. That provider may be discovered and loaded at Runtime through the same typed extension architecture used for TimingData providers, without coupling the EventData and TimingData provider families to each other. Live race state remains separate TimingNode-local state populated by ordered RaceData messages.

docs.title: IF06-REQ-013 — PING request op, answer and optional heartbeat mode
docs.text:
Type: Interface Requirement Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
IF-06 shall use one PING semantic message family with required op = REQ | ANS, optional mode = HB and optional absolute UTC message time. A PING REQUEST without mode denotes an explicitly initiated/manual check; no MANUAL value is required. When present, time denotes the creation/send time of that specific PING message. A PING ANSWER therefore creates its own message time and shall not reuse the request's time as the answer time.

The receiver of a valid PING REQUEST shall send one PING ANSWER preserving the request's mode (including its absence) as part of processing the request, without waiting for the 30-second heartbeat schedule. A PING with op = ANS shall not itself be answered. This applies in both directions. Unknown mode values shall not silently be treated as manual checks. No separate PONG message type, PING sequence number or correlation identifier is mandated by the interface; a representation/implementation may add optional correlation. Reference producers should populate time, while readers remain compatible with PING messages that omit it. PING REQUEST/ANSWER shall not consume TimingData sequence identity or create TimingData/LogBook records.

docs.title: IF06-REQ-016 — Define StageStartTimes reference semantics
docs.text:
Type: Interface Requirement Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Central shall retain StageStartTimes source state by StageId and RegistrationId. STAGE_STARTS shall carry the routed current-stage projection as incremental RegistrationId-scoped stage-start-time changes. The message itself carries neither LocationId nor StageId.

Under the current event mapping, Stage N finishes at LocationId N. Central uses the addressed TimingNode's current OPEN LocationId to select Stage N before constructing STAGE_STARTS. The RegistrationId is the timing-domain identity whose start is being defined; consumers shall not need an intermediate TeamId lookup to match a registration to its stage start. A SET shall carry one TimingTimestamp value containing at least local race time-of-day. The timestamp may also contain a local date or already be absolute when the source knows that information. A source that knows only time-of-day shall remain valid; no transport or codec layer shall invent a date or time zone. DEL removes the current definition. Elapsed-time and race-time-zone interpretation belong to SI-01 domain behaviour, not to transport or codec layers.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
When an upstream semantic connection is established or re-established, SI-01 shall first publish its current downstream receive position through RECV and shall publish its current TIMING_DATA source head through SEQ. RECV position 0 means this SI-01 runtime has not processed a normal DN_PACKET and therefore requests a full current-state resend. A positive RECV position N means SI-01 has already processed DN_PACKET N; a Central peer that has no local downstream baseline shall continue normal numbering at N+1 rather than restart at packet 1. This receive-position announcement preserves TimingNode-owned downstream state across transport reconnects and Central-process restarts.

When Central is behind the reported TIMING_DATA source head, Central shall send TIMING_DATA_REQ from its next expected sequence. When Central's processed position already equals SI-01's source head, Central need not send either an empty TIMING_DATA_REQ or an equal-position SEQ notification.

Proactive live TIMING_DATA forwarding shall normally remain enabled while the session is available. When SI-01 handles a TIMING_DATA_REQ it shall temporarily pause proactive live forwarding, capture its current LogBook head, replay through that captured head, and resume proactive live forwarding from the next sequence only after that replay completes. SEQ position exchange itself shall not gate proactive live forwarding.

TEAM_ASSIGNMENTS and STAGE_STARTS recovery shall not depend on a retained Central source sequence. When SI-01 cannot trust its downstream state it may request a full resend of the current Central-owned downstream state through RECV position 0.

docs.text: PresentationGateway is the shared entry point for presentation requests. It is owned by the Application layer; Presentation in the name identifies the adjacent side whose traffic the gateway mediates, not the layer that owns it. This uses the same directional naming principle as UpstreamGateway, while the two remain separate responsibilities: PresentationGateway is transport-independent application access and UpstreamGateway owns external upstream transport/integration. docs.title: SI01-REQ-049 — Contain TimingNode recovery failure
docs.text:
Type: Requirement Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context

This is a derived portal page. Engineering meaning is maintained in the authored Need, not in this generated presentation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A failure while restoring or validating recoverable state for one configured TimingNode shall not by itself prevent independently functioning TimingNodes or diagnostic interfaces from starting and remaining available.

For the affected TimingNode, SI-01 shall:

  • retain its independent functional OPEN/CLOSED state and LocationId;
  • continue functional behaviour that does not depend on the failed component;
  • return an explicit failure for operations that require the unavailable or failed component;
  • continue starting/running the application and its diagnostic presentation interfaces; and
  • keep independently functioning TimingNodes available in a multi-node composition.

The failure remains owned by the recovery/LogBook path and diagnostic logging. An implementation-internal TimingNode startup/execution readiness value is separate from child-component health: a LogBook recovery failure shall not by itself put that node execution state in ERROR. Such internal readiness is not part of the public current-state contract in SI01-REQ-024.

docs.title: Definition

A later inventory demand is created at least when: - a mapped TimingNode changes from not requiring inventory to OPEN; or - an operator/API operation explicitly requests another inventory/start attempt.

A registration admitted before that transition may still complete; a registration arriving after the transition shall be rejected even when antenna inventory is still stopping asynchronously.

docs.text:
Type: Requirement Comparison workspace: open object comparison workspace Source definition: open authored source Engineering Explorer: open with architecture context
